messages.text: So you're seriously taking their side? They handed me a tray with half the meal missing and then acted like I was ordering extras.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: I'm taking the side of what's written down where people actually pay. Can we just move on and pay before this line reaches the napkins?

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: That's convenient. As long as a sign exists somewhere near the cash drawer, nobody in the back can ever be wrong.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: That's not what I said. You're turning this into a trial over one scoop of potatoes.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Because the scoop was supposed to be included. They ran out, didn't say anything, and now somehow I'm the one doing advanced math at checkout.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: The sign literally says substitutions cost extra today. It isn't carved in mystery code.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: And I'm saying the sign is beside the point if they changed the deal after the tray was already in my hands. You keep acting like the only thing that counts is whatever the register gets to claim.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Because the register is where the charge happens, Hayden. The cashier didn't invent a fee just to ruin your lunch.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: I didn't say she invented it. I said the cafeteria handled it badly, and you're making it sound airtight when it wasn't.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: You're arguing like this is a courtroom and everybody behind us is the jury. It was confusing, sure, but that doesn't make your version the official replay.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: My version is what happened before we got stuck here debating poster board. If you'd been the one holding the tray, you'd be saying the same thing.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: I watched the cashier put that sign up after they ran out of the side you wanted, and I'm not saying you made it up. I'm saying the situation changed. Let's just split the extra charge and sit down.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You saw them put it up? Okay, that's different from just pointing at it like it descended from heaven. They still should've said something at the counter.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Yeah, they should've said it sooner. I'm not giving them a gold medal for communication.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Fine. Split it, then we can retire from cafeteria law before these people start charging us rent for the floor space.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Deal. Next time you pick the table first, and I'll go investigate any suspicious handwritten signage like it's breaking news.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Perfect, you've finally found your calling. Come on, let's sit before the fries get cold and this turns into your whole campaign.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Can you keep your pen from doing that for one second? It's louder in here than it should be. Also... there's something I need to tell you.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Wow, okay. What's going on? You keep staring at the same paragraph like it insulted you.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: It's not about the paragraph. I just didn't want to say it while people were still settling in. Can we finish this section first?

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: If it's about the project, just say it. We can change whatever needs changing. I can redo my part of the outline if that's where this is headed.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: No, your part is fine. That's not what this is. I just need a second to say it right.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: You're doing the quiet voice and not looking at me, so it's kind of hard not to fill in the blanks. Did I miss something? Or make this weird somehow?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: You didn't miss anything with the assignment. I thought you were asking because of the deadline stuff. I wasn't trying to make you sit there guessing.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Then what am I supposed to think? You say there's something you need to tell me, and then you keep putting it off. Did I do something wrong?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: No. No, that's not it at all. I should've just said it sooner—this isn't about you, or us working together.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Okay. Then just tell me. I'm listening.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: I'm dropping this class next week. Things at home changed fast, and I need more work hours, so this is probably the last assignment I'm doing for it. I didn't know how to drop that on you in the middle of chapter seven.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Oh. I thought you were about to tell me you were done dealing with me. That's a lot heavier than a bad group project conversation.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: I know. When you asked that, it landed really badly on my end. I wasn't trying to leave you hanging like that.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: You don't have to make it sound neat for me. We can figure out what this means for the assignment after. Are you going to be okay with work and everything?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: It'll be messy for a bit, but at least it's decided now. I emailed the professor this morning and kept rewriting how to tell you. I didn't want you hearing it like it was just logistics.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Thanks for telling me here instead of disappearing after submission. We'll finish this one, and then you can send me whatever the professor says. And next time you start with 'there's something I need to tell you,' maybe don't make me sit through four centuries first.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Cameron, not now. The line for coffee is backing into this table, and I was just leaving. Can this wait?

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Sit down for one minute. There's an empty chair, and I'm not asking for a whole afternoon. You can spare sixty seconds to answer something directly.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: You don't get to appoint a minute and call it simple. I've got my notebook, my bag, and half the cafeteria trying to get through here. Pick another time.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Interesting that another time always shows up right when I'm in front of you. If you have something to say about me anywhere else, you can manage one sentence to me.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: There it is. You drop your tray across from me like you're claiming the table, and now I'm supposed to perform on cue between the ketchup bottles and the dishwasher noise. No.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: I'm not asking for a performance. I'm asking why basic honesty suddenly requires a calendar invite when it's me.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Because ambushing somebody in a cafeteria is not the same thing as honesty. You don't get extra credit for doing it with an audience and a pointed finger at an empty chair.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: If I had texted, it would've sat there unanswered until next week. If I'd asked nicely from three tables over, you'd still be halfway to the door. So yes, I sat here.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: You keep talking like this is some test I'm trying to fail. I stood up because I'm leaving, not because you found the dramatic angle first. Move the tray and let me through.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: You make everything sound unreasonable when someone doesn't let you drift out of reach. I'm not moving until you stop pretending this is just bad timing.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I am not walking away from you; I just got a message that my advisor moved our meeting up. That's why I grabbed my notebook and stood up before you even sat down. This isn't some coded statement.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Then why have you been telling people I dodge conversations? If this is all a schedule problem, where did that come from?

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Who told you that? Because what I said was that whenever things get heated, you switch to polite logistics and call it closure. That isn't the same sentence.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: It travels the same once it leaves your mouth. I heard that I'd been turned into somebody who can't handle a real exchange, and I wasn't going to hear that secondhand and smile over soup.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Fine. That's at least a real topic. But blocking my exit before saying any of it made this look like something else entirely.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: You were already halfway gone, and it looked exactly like every other time a hard sentence was about to land. I got that part wrong about the meeting. The rest still doesn't sit right.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I have to go upstairs in about thirty seconds. If you want the exact wording and not the recycled version, send a time tonight and I'll answer it then. Not here, and not while they're calling ticket numbers over the speaker.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Tonight, then. I'm holding you to exact wording, and I'm bringing my own. Go to your meeting.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Is this spot free? I grabbed two coffees and the line over there was ridiculous. The path's crowded enough without me hovering.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: Yeah, it's free. You can sit. Just watch the backpack.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Thanks. I'm Parker. That truck across from the brick building has been blocking half the curb for twenty minutes.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: Quinn. Do you live around here? It does seem committed to making the street unusable.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: A few doors down, technically starting today. Same building as the truck, actually. Are they still telling people the elevator works better in the afternoon, or was that just leasing-office optimism?

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: They said a lot of things with a straight face. Afternoon was one of them. I haven't tested the elevator's moral character yet.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Fair. I like to know the failure points before I start carrying boxes. If your stuff's on that truck, I can at least tell you the side door sticks unless you pull hard.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: That's useful. Mine is on that truck, yeah. Timing got a little compressed.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Then you've got the fun part ahead. Did they give you the full key set, or just the front and apartment key? The mail key was mysteriously missing when I picked mine up.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: Front and apartment. No mail key. Maybe it's part of the building's personality.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Good to know it's not selective chaos. I can call management again if they keep pretending that's normal. Better to get the small things sorted before they pile up.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: You sound prepared. That's probably efficient. Saves surprises later.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: I try. Though, for the record, I actually brought this second coffee for you after I spotted you from the lease office. You looked like you could use something better than bench-level air.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: I thought you were sizing me up because of the truck and trying to see if I'd be a problem. So this is a much nicer explanation. Also, thanks.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: No, nothing like that. I recognized you from signing papers and figured walking up empty-handed would be weirder. And if anyone's a problem, it's that moving company parking like they own the zip code.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: That tracks better than the version I had. I was coming off a phone call that made the whole move sound like a spectacularly bad equation, so apparently I started assigning motives to coffee. Sorry about that.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: No need. Moving brings out a lot of unsolicited expertise from people who aren't carrying any boxes. Once the truck's done and the keys situation is fixed, the place will probably look a lot less dramatic.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: I'd like that outcome. And the coffee helps your case as a person to share a kitchen with. If you still mean it about the side door and the management calls, I may stop assuming every practical question is an inspection.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: You've been staring at that crack in the sidewalk for five minutes. And you left my messages sitting there all week. Why have you been avoiding me?

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I wasn't trying to make it look like that. Things have just been... strange lately. I didn't really know what to say.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: We're on a bench after school like we're about to discuss a lab disaster. So I'm guessing this isn't nothing. I've been trying to figure out what I did.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: You didn't do anything. It's not that simple. I just needed a little time.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Time for what, exactly? Because every time I came over by your locker, you found somewhere else to be. That usually means something specific.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: It's not really about school stuff. Or not only that, I guess. I don't know how to put it without making it worse.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: That doesn't clear anything up. It mostly sounds like you've already decided to keep me at arm's length and hand me a vague explanation for it. If something's wrong, I'd rather hear the actual version.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I'm not trying to hand you anything. I just didn't want this to turn into one of those conversations where everything changes the second it's said out loud. Can you not push for one minute?

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: I've been giving you space all week. All that did was make this weirder. If you're upset, I need you to just say it directly.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I'm not mad at you. My family might be moving, and I didn't know how to tell you. There's a chance I won't be here next month.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Oh. That's not even close to what I thought this was. Is it definite, or are they still deciding?

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Still deciding, apparently. Which somehow makes it worse, because everything stays normal while it doesn't feel normal at all. I kept thinking if I waited a little longer, maybe I wouldn't have to say it.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: So all the disappearing wasn't about me. That helps, even if the rest of it doesn't. You could've told me before it got to the point where I was inventorying every conversation we've had since Monday.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I know. Every time I almost did, it sounded too final, like saying it would make the boxes show up at the door. And you looked so normal every day that I couldn't bring myself to drop this in the middle of calculus.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Calculus would have been a terrible setting, to be fair. This bench isn't exactly ideal either, but at least now I know why you've been acting like I set your backpack on fire. If it happens, we can figure out what not losing contact looks like.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: That sounds a lot better than what I was expecting to hear. Nothing's settled yet, so maybe it's all noise for nothing. But thanks for not making me drag this out any longer.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: You needed something before you head out? I'm still updating the notes from that meeting, so make it quick. The cabinet key's here if this is about supplies.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Actually, both things. I just need the conference room for a bit to spread these class packets out, and the markers from the cabinet. The schedule on the wall looks open, so I figured I should grab it now before someone wanders in.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: Hold on a second. Which time slot are you looking at? The board and the computer were not matching a minute ago.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Right now, through the next hour. It still looks blank up there. If it's open there, why can't I use it now?

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: I'm not saying you can't use a room just to be difficult. I'm saying I need to check what actually went through. The wall schedule is not always caught up after these meetings.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Okay, but from here it just looks available. And you paused like there was already some no lined up before I even asked. I only need enough space to sort handouts and label a few folders.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: Because when people see an empty line on that sheet, they start treating it like a first-come claim. Then I get three versions of the same argument at once. Let me pull up the update instead of doing this from across the desks.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: I'm not trying to start a whole thing. I'm just standing here with a folder and a deadline, and the posted slot still looks open. If there's a reason, just give me the reason.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: Fine, come look. I booked that room right after the meeting for the department check-in, so it is not actually open. The calendar just refreshed, and the entry is there now.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Oh. That explains why you kept looking back at the wall like it was wrong. I thought this was turning into one of those weird room standoffs.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: No, it's just bad timing with the update. The posting lagged behind by a couple of minutes, that's all. If you still need space, let's find something that won't get bumped.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Yeah, that's on me. I saw the blank line and ran with it. Is there another room free, or should I just take the markers and camp at an empty desk somewhere?

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: Small room by the copy area is open until three, and nobody usually touches it after lunch. Take the markers, the extra tape, and the blue sign-out sheet from the cabinet so nobody chases you down later. If you need the larger table, I can put you in the conference room after the check-in ends.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: The small room works. And the sign-out sheet is probably smart, since apparently I was already halfway to causing paperwork drama. After three would actually help for the bigger stack anyway.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: I'll add your name for three-thirty so it's clear on both calendars. Grab what you need now, and leave the key on my desk when you're done with the cabinet. That should keep everyone from circling back over the same question.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Perfect. Thanks for sorting it out without making me guess anymore. I'll take the tape, markers, and sheet, and I'll be out of your way in a second.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: The deadline is right here on the screen, and the clock is not doing anyone favors. If we leave now, I can maybe finish the short answers in the car before check-in. I'm not sitting in this conference room arguing over printouts.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: You are not running out the door before we sort this out. Put the bag down and look at these schedules for one minute. The laptop isn't the only thing on the table today.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: This is exactly why I need to decide for myself. That timestamp doesn't move because you want a family meeting with stapled pages. If we miss the window, nobody at the tournament is going to care why.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: And nobody there is going to benefit from you flying out of your chair halfway through a sentence. I laid out the route, the hotel, and the check-in time for a reason. Every time I point to one page, you point harder at the screen.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Because the screen is the thing that locks in first. You're acting like this application is some extra errand I invented to make the morning difficult. I need to leave before this turns into one more lecture and one less opportunity.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: What turns it into a lecture is you grabbing that duffel bag every thirty seconds like the door is the only solution. Sit down long enough to act like timing matters in both directions. The trip doesn't disappear because you're impatient.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Impatient? The portal closes today, not next week. If I wait for you to finish walking me through highlighted departure times, I'll be explaining to everyone later why I let somebody else's schedule make the choice for me.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Somebody else's schedule? We are talking about a commitment you already made, not a random suggestion on my clipboard. You keep saying there's no choice here, but all I see is you trying to bolt before we put things in order.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Order doesn't help if the order is wrong. You keep circling that check-in line like it's the only deadline in the room. It sounds a lot like the application can just take the hit as long as nobody messes with your plan.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Don't tell me what I sound like when you're the one refusing to listen past your own countdown. I have been trying to keep this whole day from turning into a wreck. You don't get to rewrite that because I won't wave you out the door.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Then stop blocking the only workable option. Every minute we're standing here, the odds get worse, and you know that. If the point is to make me choose the team over the application, just say it without all the paper shuffling.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: I already called the organizer. Check-in can be an hour late, so sit down and submit the application now, and then we leave together. Put the bag by the chair and use the time for the thing that actually closes.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: You called them already? An hour late still counts? Then why didn't you start with that instead of making this sound like I was trying to pull something?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Because every time I opened my mouth, you were halfway to the hallway. And from where I was standing, all the finger-pointing at that date looked a lot more like a dare than a plan. Open the application and get to the last page.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Fine. The essay box is done, I just need the activities section and the upload. If the check-in really has that cushion, then hand me the folder after I hit submit so I can make sure I didn't miss anything else.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: That's better. Finish the upload, then we'll go over the route in two minutes and head out. I can read the checklist while you attach the transcript.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: The transcript's already in the downloads folder. If the wifi in here doesn't stall, this can be done before your two minutes are up. And for the record, the bag stays packed.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: The bag can stay packed. Hit submit, close the laptop, and we'll leave together. Next time, lead with the page that's on fire, and I'll do the same.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Seat's open. Watch the coffee, the table wobbles if you set too much on that side.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Good catch. This place always has one leg shorter than the others, and somehow it's always the table I pick. You surviving the lunch rush, or did you hide out in the corner on purpose?

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: It's quieter here. Soup's decent today, if you ignore the bread.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I already made the mistake with the bread. Should've traded for chips. How's your day been upstairs?

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Fine. Printer jammed twice, then stopped pretending it worked.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Sounds about right for this building. Yesterday kind of went off the rails for me too.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Yeah. Seemed like it.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: You were pretty quiet when I got in last night. Then this morning too. I can usually tell when the apartment's doing that weird echo thing where nobody wants to start the sentence.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: There was a bill due. Still true this morning.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I know. I wasn't acting like it didn't matter.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Didn't look urgent. You came in late, dropped your bag, said something about today being crazy, and left it there. Then today it's weather and cafeteria bread.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Because if I opened with it in the kitchen at midnight, it would've turned into a whole thing before I could get two words out. And right now you're looking at me like you've already got the story finished.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Then go ahead. I'm here.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: You think I just blew off the bill, but I got pulled into a client emergency. Here—look at this. Yesterday, 2:17, they reassigned me and everything after that went sideways.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Let me see. ...Okay, that's not small. You printed the whole email.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I figured saying it out loud would sound convenient. I still should've sent one text before it got late, even if it was just "can't deal with anything else right now."

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: That would've helped. I filled it this morning so it wouldn't roll into a fee, but this makes yesterday look different.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I'll transfer you the money this afternoon, and the late coffee too. Next time if work drops a piano on one of us, let's do a one-line warning so the other person's not guessing all night.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: The TV's been flashing captions at us for ten minutes, and you've been staring at that mug like it owes you money. Those envelopes have been sitting on the coffee table since lunch. Open them now.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: They'll still be there in five minutes. You don't have to run the room every time paper shows up. Let me finish this first.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: That's exactly how things pile up. One thing waits, then three more wait, then suddenly somebody's late on something important. I'm not watching that routine again.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: It's not a routine. And not everything needs commentary the second it lands in the house. We can talk about something else for a minute.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: No, we can talk about the stack in front of you. You glanced at it the second you sat down, so don't act like it's junk mail. If there's a problem, say what the problem is.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: There isn't a problem. You're turning envelopes into a whole hearing. Can you just leave it alone for one second?

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You get quiet, then snappy, then somehow I'm the one making a scene. If this is about a bill, a deadline, whatever, you don't fix it by pretending the table is invisible. Open it.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: It's not about pretending anything. I was going to say something. You just don't give anything a chance to arrive on its own.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Then say it. Because from where I'm sitting, this looks like you waiting me out until I get tired and stop asking. That's not happening.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: I wasn't waiting you out. I wanted two minutes without being cornered over paperwork. That's all.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Paperwork matters when it affects the people in this house. You don't get to go vague and call it privacy whenever something inconvenient shows up. Hand me the top one if you're not going to do it.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Shiloh, don't. I'll handle it. Just put it back.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: "Westlake Systems"? And this says "Relocation Packet." Cameron, what is this. Why is there a housing packet in our living room?

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: I already accepted the job and I'm moving next month. I was going to tell you tonight. Not like this, but tonight.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Next month. You signed onto a whole move, got the packet mailed here, sat across from me, and let me go on about envelopes like an idiot. How long has this been decided?

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Long enough for the letter to catch up, not long enough for any version of this to get easier. I was trying to come in with something more than a sentence dropped between commercials. You were supposed to hear it from me, not from a company logo.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You had plenty of chances before a logo got there first. This isn't forgetting to mention some form; this is boxes, keys, a different city. Do Mom and Dad know, or was I just first by accident?

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: No one got the full version yet. I wanted to line up the apartment, the date, all of it, so I wasn't dropping chaos in everyone's lap. That part clearly didn't go the way I planned.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: I put the boxes by the filing cabinets like you asked, and the transfer form is clipped on top. The inventory lines are filled in except for your signature. If we can finish this before noon, I can take the key over right away.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Hold on a second. There was something in this folder from this morning, and I want to make sure I'm looking at the right page. Don't move those boxes yet.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: They're already half packed, so I'd rather not open everything again unless we have to. The form just needs the last approval line. Can we just finish this now?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: It's not that simple today. Let me get through these notices first. I don't want to put my name on the wrong thing.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: It's the same supply transfer sheet we used last month. I copied the cabinet numbers onto my notepad and matched them to the labels on the boxes. If this sits much longer, the handoff gets messy.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I heard you. Just give me a minute. There was a change this morning, and I need to sort out what applies before we do the handoff.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: You keep saying a minute, but the clock on your desk is doing its own thing. I already called downstairs once about the room, and they won't keep it open forever. If something's missing, I can fix it.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: It's not a missing staple, Ellis. I'm trying not to make this harder than it already is. Please stop pushing the form at me for one minute.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: I'm pushing the form because it's the only part left that needs you. The boxes are counted, the labels are on, and the cart is waiting outside. From where I'm standing, this looks like a regular sign-off turning into a whole morning.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: From where you're standing, maybe. From here, there are a few lines in this folder that change what counts as regular. I was about to say that before you slid the paper back over.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Then say it. Because right now it sounds like this can wait until after lunch, and it can't. If there's a problem, just tell me.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I am not stalling the form; I found a budget freeze notice this morning, and I may be transferring out soon, so I needed to explain why I cannot sign this the way you expect. If I put my name there now, the form could come back rejected, and then you're worse off than if I paused you here. That's what I've been trying to get out.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: You could have started with that. The room deadline is still noon, though, and those boxes need to land somewhere today. If your signature won't clear it, whose will?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Marta can approve under the freeze, or Operations can hold the transfer pending review. And if my desk gets reassigned next week, I don't want your paperwork tied to me halfway through. I should have said that before I picked up the folder again.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: All right. Marta's upstairs, but she disappears into meetings after eleven-thirty. If I carry the inventory sheet to her now, will she have enough, or do you need to add something first?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I'll note the freeze code and attach the notice so she doesn't have to chase it. Give me the form and your notepad. We can also mark the boxes as staged instead of transferred, which might keep the room request alive for today.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Staged is better than locked out. I can relabel the top two boxes if that keeps receiving from sending them back. Should I still take the cart downstairs, or leave it by your door until Marta signs?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Leave it by my door for ten minutes. Once I staple this packet, you can catch Marta before her calendar swallows her. After that, take the cart straight to receiving and show them the freeze note.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Okay. Next time, don't make me guess from a silent folder and a face over reading glasses. I thought you were brushing this off.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Fair enough. Next time, let me finish one sentence before you march the signature line across the desk. Now hand me that pen, and we'll get you upstairs before eleven-thirty.

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: Sorry, the line was ridiculous. Every person in front of me ordered something with six modifications, so now I have this dangerously adult coffee. You got here early.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I did, and now I get to judge your serious-looking coffee in peace. Mine came with enough ice to survive until next week, so I can't complain. Sit before somebody steals your tiny chair.

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: Thanks. It's louder in here than I expected, but maybe that's useful. I wanted us to be clear with each other, and in person seemed better than trying to do that over text.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Clear sounds intense for a place with a muffin case and a guy mispronouncing macchiato behind us. But yeah, in person is better. I figured we'd just see where this goes.

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: Right. So when you suggested coffee, what did you want this to be? I don't mean the beverage part.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: You really came prepared for an agenda. I don't know, I like this place, and you've got strong opinions about everything, so that seemed promising. Also your messages read way less severe than your coffee does.

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: I'm not trying to be severe. I'd just rather not let things get fuzzy and then have everybody pretend they knew what was happening later. That usually gets messy.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: You say that like there are minutes being taken somewhere. It can just be coffee first, you know. Then maybe we decide whether your scheduling energy is charming or alarming.

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: And what would count as deciding? Because you're making jokes, which is fine, but I'm asking seriously. I don't want us walking out with different versions of this.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Okay, seriously then. I asked because talking in little message bubbles was getting weirdly edited, and I wanted to see you without all that. See if this felt like something, or if we're just two people with mutual friends and decent timing.

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: I get that. And I like talking to you, but I think it's better if this stays in the lane where nobody starts building extra meaning onto it. That's part of why I wanted to meet sooner rather than later.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: That's a very polished lane metaphor. Usually when people say something like that, they leave at least one exit open. Are you doing that, or is this one of those speeches with the answer buried in the middle?

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: I'm saying I'd rather keep this simple. You're easy to spend time with, and I'd rather not complicate that. It doesn't need to become a whole thing.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: You're making it sound like I brought a contract. I asked you to coffee, Blake, not a joint mortgage. If you asked me here just to tell me not to get the wrong idea, you could have said that sooner.

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: Fine. I got back together with my ex two days ago, so romance was off the table before we met. I figured saying it face-to-face was better than letting you hear it from somebody else.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Wow. So this was cleanup. Good to know before I say anything else that makes this more embarrassing than it already is.

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: That's not what I was trying to do. You reached out, and I didn't want this drifting into something I'd have to shut down later, especially once people started talking. Meeting seemed more respectful than dodging you.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Respectful would have been leading with the only fact that actually mattered. Instead I got ten minutes of strategic wording and a lane diagram. You could've spared both of us the performance.

messages.speaker: Blake
messages.text: Maybe I handled it badly. I still don't want this to turn ugly or weird in the group, and I meant what I said about liking talking to you. I'd rather leave this as something that can still be normal.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Normal is probably ambitious for today. But you don't need to worry about me making a scene over coffee and clattering cups. Finish your serious drink; I've heard enough.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Hey, hi. Your camera's super clear—I can see the assignment doc reflected in your glasses. I usually like to start by figuring out how people work together before we dive in.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Hey. Nice, yeah, I've got the doc open already—could you send over the notes and whatever files you have for the project? Then we can split things up fast.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Totally, we can get there. I just like knowing whether someone's more outline-first or draft-first, because group projects get weird otherwise. Are you the kind of person who wants frequent check-ins or just a clean handoff?

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Depends on the class, but probably somewhere in the middle. Could you send the notes first so we can start? The doc looks pretty bare on my end.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Yeah, the empty doc is kind of the awkward stage. I usually end up doing better with people who don't disappear for three days and then drop a paragraph at 11:58. Last semester I got burned by that, so now I ask stuff up front.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Fair. I'd rather not do the mystery teammate thing either. But if you have material ready, sending it now would help a lot.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Okay, so you're more 'get the engine running and talk while it's moving.' I can work with that. When you do your part, do you want comments as you go, or do you prefer to finish a section and then compare?

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Either is fine as long as we're looking at the same stuff. Right now we're kind of discussing a kitchen I haven't been let into yet. If there's a folder, that would make this easier.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: You make it sound like I'm guarding the pantry. I'm not trying to make this weird; I just like knowing who I'm building with. Some people are great at the work and awful at the actual partnering part.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: I'm not asking for your social security number, just the project files. I just need the folder now because I have another deadline tonight. Once I can see what you've got, we can do the whole rhythm-and-process conversation.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Oh, I already set everything up and was waiting to share it until I knew how you liked to work. That's on me. Hold on—I'm dropping the folder link in the chat now, with the notes, source list, and a draft outline.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Okay, wow, that is actually a very different problem than the one I thought we were having. Got it. Thanks for sending it—next time, lead with 'I already made the folder' and I become instantly charming.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Noted. I probably made that way more elaborate than it needed to be. The outline's color-coded, which now feels a little intense seeing your face.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: No, color-coded is good—color-coded says you care, which is useful. I can take the intro and the comparison section tonight, and if your notes cover the case study part, we can stitch it together tomorrow. Comments in the doc work better than long text threads for me.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: That actually works really well. I already pulled quotes for the case study, so I'll slot those into a separate page and tag you where the comparison section connects. And for the record, I don't vanish for three days.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Excellent, then we're ahead of the average group project by several geological eras. I'll draft tonight after I finish the other thing, and you'll see comments as I go. This is definitely more workable now.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: No, listen, that's the part everyone skips. If the city puts the lights in along this path, people will actually use the park after sunset instead of cutting through once and never coming back.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Mm. It is nicer over here by the pond, though. We could sit for a second if you want.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Exactly, that's what I'm saying—the place already does half the work. You add a few benches, a little lighting, and suddenly it stops feeling like dead space and starts feeling like somewhere people choose.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You really came prepared for a park walk. Did you rehearse this, or do I just bring out your campaign speeches?

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Rude. Also a little fair. But seriously, when people say nobody cares about public space, I think they just haven't seen what happens when one person makes a case for it properly.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You're definitely making a case. I just pointed at a bench and somehow got a full presentation.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Because the bench is Exhibit A. Empty, good view of the water, right by the walking path—it's perfect, and nobody treats it like it matters.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Maybe it matters for reasons that don't fit on your little proposal board. Sometimes a bench is just a bench, and sometimes it isn't.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Okay, now you sound mysterious on purpose. I'm just saying the design changes how people act, and then they tell themselves it was spontaneous.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: And I'm saying not everything needs a thesis attached to it. Some things can just happen if you let them.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: I know, I know, but this one actually has a point. My friend is presenting to the neighborhood board next week, and if they frame it like safety plus actual use instead of just 'beautification,' people who usually roll their eyes might finally go for it.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You really took that turn fast. I wasn't trying to set up a committee meeting.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Oh. I thought you were teeing me up, because you did that look-like-you're-listening thing and then the bench, so I figured you wanted the whole argument.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I was kind of hoping we could sit for a minute and just be together.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Sure, let's sit first, and then I can tell you the short version.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: The short version I can do. Come here—this side has the better view, unless you're about to argue with the pond too.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: The pond can keep its dignity for one evening. Short version: if they pitch it as making places people actually linger in, not just prettier paths, they'll get more support.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: That does sound smarter. And lingering seems like a pretty solid use of a place.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Right, exactly. Also, I probably should've noticed you weren't giving me debate-face—you were giving me the other kind.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Well, now you've got the short version of mine too. Let's see if you do any better with fewer footnotes.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Hi. The desk line looks longer every time I look at it. Did they already give you your room key?

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Yes. It took about three minutes. They hand over the packet with the keycard and the schedule.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Good to know. I kept thinking I was in the wrong place because everyone here looks like they know where to go. Is the program packet actually clear, or is it one of those folders with six maps and no answers?

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: It's organized enough. The first page has tomorrow's check-in times and room numbers. Do you already know your schedule, or are you still sorting logistics?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Still sorting, apparently. I have pieces of it written down, but seeing a hotel ballroom labeled with three different event signs did not improve anything. You probably got through it without orbiting the lobby twice.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: The signs are bad, not you. Registration is through those doors past the seating area, and the elevators are behind the desk. If you want, sit for a minute before getting in line again.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Thanks. I might, unless your suitcase means you're about to disappear upstairs. I don't want to intercept your evening just because I arrived looking misplaced.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I'm not rushing anywhere. Check-in just finished before you walked over. I can stay a few minutes.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: A few minutes is enough to rescue a first day. Is it usually this overwhelming at the start, or do people just pretend they aren't reading the same sign five times? Do the returning students ever help people settle in, or is everyone expected to figure it out quietly?

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Some people help if they're asked. Most of the confusion burns off once tomorrow starts and the schedule becomes real. The first evening is mostly noise and luggage.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You seem like someone who already knows how this place works. Like you'd spot the hidden table with the right forms before anyone else does. I mean, you don't look rattled by any of this.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I've been in enough buildings like this to know they all hide the same table somewhere. And for what it's worth, the first hour here catches almost everyone off balance. You don't look unprepared; you look like you're trying to get your footing before the crowd decides it for you.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: That's a better description than orbiting the lobby twice. I brought this notebook so I'd seem less scattered, and now it's mostly a prop with arrows in it. The crowd part is accurate, unfortunately.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: The notebook is useful. Half the people here are pretending they remember everything after hearing it once, and they won't by breakfast. If you want, we can compare tomorrow's schedule once you get your packet, just to make sure the arrows match reality.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You'd really do that? I figured you had your own setup and didn't need a stray person attaching themselves to it. Most people get polite when they want to be left alone.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: If I wanted to leave, I'd have picked up the suitcase and done it already. I'd rather start with one person who knows where the room is than watch ten people pretend they do. Besides, this week will go more smoothly if at least one familiar face isn't guessing.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: That's unexpectedly kind. I can manage my own confusion once I know which part of it is normal. Having one familiar face sounds less dramatic than what my notebook has been preparing for.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Then let's make it boring on purpose. After you check in, take the packet back here and we'll sort the important parts first: breakfast time, opening session, and whichever room they've renamed since printing the map. After that, the lobby can keep being theatrical without dragging you into it.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Deal. And if I come back with three different papers and a defeated expression, you'll know the desk won. Thank you for not making this feel like a test I started failing before saying hello.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Hotel desks do that to people; it's not a character measure. Bring whatever they hand you, and we'll untangle it. Tomorrow is easier once the pieces have names.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: You can stop tracking raindrops on the window and tell me whether dinner was really that bad. Traffic's going nowhere anyway. We've got time before I turn onto the highway.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Dinner was dinner. Aunt Denise asked the same question six different ways, so that part was predictable. It's not really about tonight.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: You've been off with me all night, haven't you? Every time I came near the kitchen, you suddenly needed a refill or a napkin. So if this isn't about Denise, what is it about?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I said it's not about tonight. I was trying to find a window where Mom wasn't hovering three feet away. That house has terrible acoustics for anything that matters.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Okay. Then use the car. The radio's off, nobody else is here, and we're trapped behind a minivan with a dented bumper, so there are no distractions.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: A lot is going to change soon. I kept waiting for there to be some cleaner way to say that, but apparently there isn't one.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: That's a pretty dramatic opener for someone who claimed it wasn't about tonight. Change how? Work, family, or the category where I'm supposed to guess and get it wrong?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Work is part of it. Timing is part of it. And before you do that thing where you turn one sentence into a closing argument, let me finish.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: That thing? Good to know my best qualities are still getting airtime. Just say it directly.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I'm trying to. You don't exactly make these conversations easy when you grip the wheel like you're about to cross-examine me.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Because you're talking like somebody about to hand me a verdict. First it's not dinner, then it's a lot is changing, then I'm the problem with the steering wheel. If you're mad at me, just say it.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I'm not mad at you. I already accepted a job in Seattle, and I was trying to figure out how to tell you before everyone else finds out.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Seattle. That's not exactly a longer commute. And 'already accepted' is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: The offer came through last week. I signed yesterday. I wanted you to hear it from me before Mom turned it into a group announcement with pie.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Two months from now, or two months from six months ago? Because those are different conversations. You had me thinking this ride was about something I'd done.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Two months from now. And this ride was about me not wanting the first version you heard to come from the family grapevine. I knew there was a decent chance you'd hear 'Seattle' and then fill in the rest with everybody else's favorite words.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: So that's what this was. Not punishment. Just late notice with a zip code attached.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You got late notice because I wanted one conversation without commentary from the back row. It's a good job, Charlie. And it doesn't erase my phone, the airport, or your talent for showing up uninvited and reorganizing my kitchen.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: I only reorganized it because you kept the spices next to the plates like a maniac. Seattle's far, Harper. I can work with far, but not with finding out after everyone else starts pretending they saw it coming.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Then don't make me regret starting here. Nobody else knows yet. You do, and when they start in with their speeches, you can remind me why leaving town doesn't require vanishing.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: You can take that chair if you want. The window's less noisy than the middle tables, unless the espresso machine starts up again. I was just deciding whether this coffee counts as coffee.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I'll risk it. Actually, this is good timing—I wanted to catch you about the client intake workflow before the meeting tomorrow. I think we're about to make it more complicated than it needs to be.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Mm. The current draft does have a lot of steps in it. What part are you looking at changing?

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: The approval layer in the middle, mostly. If we move the exception flags earlier, ops wouldn't have to stop every standard request, and the team would spend less time cleaning up duplicates. It could really use your backing, because people actually listen when you point out where the logic breaks.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Maybe. There are a few ways that could play out. Sorry—go on.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Right, so imagine the intake form scoring requests before they hit the queue. The obvious cases keep moving, the unusual ones get routed for review, and nobody has to pretend every item needs the same level of scrutiny. It would save time without making us look careless.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I can see the appeal. The edge cases are where these things usually get attacked, though.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: That's why I mapped examples. The nonprofit accounts, the international ones, the duplicate vendor records—those would still trigger review. So are you with me on this, at least in principle?

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I'm not sure. It depends what room that argument lands in.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: What room? This is still just our team discussion, isn't it? I'm not asking you to walk into someone else's meeting and plant a flag.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I'm saying context matters. People hear 'streamline' and start filling in their own version of what gets cut.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: That's exactly why I wanted to talk it through with you first. But you've barely looked at me since I sat down, so I'm guessing something in this sounds thinner out loud than it did in my head.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: No, that's not— I mean, the examples are fine. I'm just tracking something.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: If this is a bad time, just tell me. I'd rather hear that than keep pitching into static.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: It's not your idea—I keep looking out there because I'm waiting to hear whether I'm being pulled onto another project, and I haven't been allowed to talk about it yet. So I've been trying not to say the wrong thing before I know what today's version of today is.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Oh. That makes a lot more sense than whatever story I was writing from the coffee stirring. You could have just said there was other traffic in the background; I wouldn't have kept leaning on it.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I probably should've said something earlier, just not the useful part. For what it's worth, the workflow change itself doesn't sound flimsy. I just can't be the clean yes-or-no machine over lunch.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Fair enough. Keep your machine off warranty until you know where you're being plugged in. When things settle, I'd still like your read on the weak spots, because I'd rather fix them with you than defend a draft nobody stress-tested.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Your food's getting cold again. You only do that when something's chewing on you harder than the waiter asking if we want dessert. So what happened?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Someone at work has been skipping a safety step to move clients through faster. It looked small the first time, and then it kept happening. Someone could actually get hurt if I stay quiet.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Is this the person with the kid and the rent mess? The one who keeps picking up extra shifts? Because that lands differently than some careless idiot cutting corners for fun.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I know exactly who it is, and I know their life is a mess right now. That doesn't make the shortcut less dangerous. There has to be accountability.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Accountability can mean more than one thing. You don't know what reporting them could do to their whole life. Going straight to management feels brutal.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: And what am I supposed to do if this keeps happening next week? Just keep watching and call that compassion? How can I justify not saying something?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You're already talking like the form is filled out and sent. Like the only real question is whether you can live with a delay. That's not the same as asking what might actually stop it.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: What stops it if they decide they can get away with it again? A private talk and crossed fingers? The clients don't get to absorb the risk so the rest of us can feel gentler.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You keep talking like being a good person just means handing someone over. Like if a system punishes them, your part comes out clean. That's a little too neat.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: And you keep talking like protecting one person matters more than the people who could get hurt. That's not neat either. If we're choosing who pays for this, I don't see why it should be the clients.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I didn't say let it slide. I said there's a difference between naming what they did to their face and dropping them into management's lap before they even get a chance to fix it. Those aren't the same kind of accountability.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Then say it plainly. If I pull them aside tomorrow and they deny it or do it again, I can't keep carrying this around like it's just a misunderstanding. There has to be a line somewhere.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Fine. Tomorrow, first thing, tell them you saw it, tell them it stops immediately, and tell them if it happens again you go up the chain. No vague hints, no rescue speech, no pretending it didn't matter.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: That sounds more honest than smiling through a shift and then filing something later. At least they hear it from me before it becomes a formal mess. And if they brush it off, then I'm not inventing an emergency out of nowhere.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Exactly. You're not covering for them, and you're not swinging the biggest hammer first. If they care at all, that warning lands hard enough.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Okay. I'll do that before lunch tomorrow, and if they push back or I catch it again, then it goes higher. Eat your fries before you start stealing mine for being dramatic.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Okay, look—this version finally ties everything together. The timeline on the planning sheet lines up with the budget notes, and the outreach piece gives it an actual public-facing payoff. If we send the draft from the laptop after one more pass, it looks polished.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Do we really have time for all three parts? The deadline is close, and the sheet already looks packed. The outreach section alone spills into the margin.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Only because I wrote small. The pieces support each other, that's the whole point. If we strip one out, it starts reading like three disconnected notes instead of a coherent project.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: How fixed is the campus event piece? I'm looking at the venue request, the partner emails, the survey, and the follow-up summary. That's a lot of moving parts for one section.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: It's the part people will remember. And it's not as huge as it looks when it's broken into steps. You always do this thing where a list on paper turns into a warning label.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: A list on paper usually becomes a calendar problem later. If outreach slips, everything after it slips too. What happens if we keep the analysis and the pilot but cut the event?

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Then we lose the section that shows we're not just keeping this inside the building. And if this is about who has to do what, we can rebalance tasks instead of chopping out the most visible part.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: It isn't just about task split. I'm asking because the current version seems broad. The first page promises a lot for ten days.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Broad isn't the same as unrealistic. The methods are already drafted, your notes cover the analysis cleanly, and I can handle the coordination calls. We don't need to shrink it every time the plan starts looking ambitious.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: You can handle the calls, sure, but the proposal still has to survive review. If someone reads this cold, they may focus on what can actually be completed by the deadline. That's why I keep coming back to outreach.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: You're circling that section like it's the weak link, but it's the part that makes the whole thing persuasive. Without it, we just have a narrower internal study with a nice spreadsheet. I need you to meet me halfway here.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: I should have mentioned this earlier: the reviewer emailed me this morning and said we need a much narrower scope, and they singled out the outreach section as too ambitious.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: They emailed you this morning? And that was sitting there while I was defending the event line by line? Okay. Fine—then the outreach piece can't stay the way it is.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: That's why I kept asking around it. I wasn't sure how to bring it up while you were walking through the full version. The rest of the note wasn't a disaster; it was mostly scope.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: All right. Then let's make it look like a deliberate refinement, not a retreat. We keep the analysis, keep the pilot, and turn outreach into a brief dissemination plan instead of an actual campus event.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: That would match the feedback better. We could replace the event logistics with a one-page summary of who we'd contact later and why. It saves space and stops the timeline from collapsing under its own weight.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Yes, and on the first page we can frame it as phased work: immediate deliverables now, broader engagement after the review period. That way it still sounds outward-looking without pretending we can run a full program in ten days. Hand me the planning sheet.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Here. I'll mark the outreach section for compression and trim the claims in the overview. Once that's done, the proposal should read a lot cleaner.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You've been rotating that glass for ten minutes. At this point the ice is getting more attention than I am. Did I miss a chapter somewhere?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: It's not a big deal. This place is just loud enough that you can pretend people aren't listening. Convenient.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Convenient for what, exactly? Because if this is about last Friday, or me leaving early, or that dumb joke outside the theater, I'll sort through the whole list.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You always have a list ready. Makes things neat. Real life doesn't usually come labeled that nicely.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Okay, just tell me what I messed up and I'll fix it. No guessing game, no dramatic reenactment, just the short version.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You think everything has a short version. Some things only make sense when you notice them before somebody spells them out.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Then help me notice. You've been half somewhere else for weeks, and every time I get close to the point, you slide the point under the table.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Have you ever felt like someone only notices when it's almost too late? Like suddenly they get very attentive once the train's already moving.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: If that's about me being late to the party, say that. If it's about me acting like an idiot, say that too. I can apologize without needing riddles first.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You tell me what this has been. All the dinners that ran long, all the almosts, all the times you looked at me like you were about to say something and then ordered another drink.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: That sounds a lot less like I forgot your birthday and a lot more like you're asking whether I've been careless with you. I haven't been passing time, Harper. I thought we were edging toward the same thing, just badly.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Edging toward. That's one way to keep the floor from appearing. Nice and safe.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Safe would be talking in circles until the bartender throws us out. I'm here asking straight. Were you waiting for me to say something first, or are you trying to make me confess to some crime I haven't identified yet?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You make it sound simple. Say the perfect line, solve the scene, everybody laughs at how weirdly tense it got. That's not really what's sitting here.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: No, it isn't simple. That's why I'm still here leaning over a sticky table while a guy behind me butchers karaoke. I don't need perfect; I need the actual thing.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I took the Seattle job, and I didn't tell you because I needed to know whether losing me would matter to you.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: It would matter, and I need honesty from you, not tests. If we're important to each other, we say the hard thing directly.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Seattle starts in six weeks. I kept picking the wrong moment, and then it started looking worse every day I waited. So here's the direct version, late as it is.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Six weeks is not nothing, but it's not a vanishing act either. Don't make me drag the truth out of you again and then wave from an airport like we're strangers who once had good timing.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Then let's not do that. We can talk about what six weeks looks like, and what comes after, without pretending it's casual or impossible.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You said you wanted to talk. I just got in. What is it?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Can you not do the doorway thing? Just for a minute. The fridge is louder than you right now.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I'm listening. I haven't even taken my jacket off yet, so if this is going to be a whole winding setup, skip to the part that matters.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: It does matter. That's why I'm trying not to say it badly. Could you maybe not make it sound like I'm starting a fight before I've said anything?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Then say it. You've got the mug clutched like somebody died, and you're looking at me like there's a test at the end of this.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: There kind of is. Not like that. I just need to know you'll actually hear me before you start deciding what this is about.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: That usually means you've already decided what answer you want. If this is about where things are going or whether I'm around enough, don't turn it into some ceremony in the kitchen.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: You really think that's all I'd stop you for? You come in, drop your bag, keep your shoes on, and suddenly I'm the one making a scene.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You're the one saying it like there's broken glass under every word. So what, you want promises? A calendar? Just say the actual problem.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Fine. I took two tests this morning, and both were positive.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: The pharmacy tests? You're sure they weren't expired or something. You took two?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Yes, the pharmacy tests. Two different boxes, because I already knew you'd ask me that first. They're on the bathroom counter if you want proof arranged by sink.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: No, I don't need to inspect them. Did you call a doctor yet, or is this just from this morning?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Just this morning. I was waiting until you got home before I did anything else. You looked like I was trying to corner you over dishes or feelings.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I didn't know this was what you meant. That's different. We don't have to decide everything standing here next to the fruit bowl.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: No, we don't. But standing here is what we've got, and you're still half dressed like you're about to leave again. So tell me something real.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I'm here, aren't I? First thing is confirming it properly. After that, we deal with what needs dealing with.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: That sounds neat, but you're talking like a checklist. Is there some other thing you're not putting on the counter with the keys and the backpack?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: There are a few things I haven't gotten into yet. Tonight got crowded fast. Let me get through the next five minutes before you start opening every drawer at once.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I'm not opening drawers. I'm standing in our kitchen telling you something that changes everything, and you're talking around corners. If there's another sentence in this house that belongs in this conversation, don't save it for later.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Is this station always this fuzzy, or is your car just choosing today to sound haunted? Every light on this road takes forever. We could probably age a year before the next green.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: My car has standards and rejects bad radio with drama. Hand me that water bottle by your feet, would you? How was the rest of your day after lunch?

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Mostly normal. Long, boring, fluorescent-light normal. Why, did somebody suddenly start giving out medals for attendance?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: No medals, tragic as that is. You just look like you're rehearsing a speech to the windshield. If there's a headline, go ahead and print it.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Maybe I'm just tired. And this phone keeps sliding out of my hands because the case is cracked. Not everything has a headline.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Mm-hm. Funny thing about 'nothing' is how much noise it can make when someone keeps flipping it over like that. Did anything happen at school this week I should hear from you instead of from the universe?

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: That sounds weirdly specific. Did the universe start calling parents now? I mean, school is school, people are annoying, classes are classes.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: The universe has bureaucracy now, apparently. I'm asking you, not people, not classes. You.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Okay, well, there was some stuff. Not, like, catastrophe stuff. Just a couple things that got sideways.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: A couple things can mean a spilled coffee or a police report. Pick a lane. Start with the one that's making you sand that phone smooth.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Can you not do the lawyer voice right now? I was going to say it, I just wanted to get through one red light without making this worse. It has to do with school.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Then say it straight. No trailers, no teaser campaign.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: I need to tell you something about school. It wasn't one thing, exactly, and I wasn't trying to turn it into some giant—

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: The counselor already called me about the skipped classes, Lennox, so I need the whole truth now. Not the version that trims the edges off.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: They already called you? Then what was all of this for? You had me sitting here talking about radio stations and lunch like this was any normal ride home.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Because there was a difference between hearing it from them and hearing it from you. And right now I'm still waiting on the second one. How many classes?

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Two. This week. I left campus with Mara after second period on Tuesday, and then again Thursday, and this phone is hers because mine died and I didn't want a call coming in where I'd have to explain it in the hallway.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: So this took planning, not one bad five-minute impulse. Why those days, and don't hand me 'I don't know.' If there was more than skipping, now is the time.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Tuesday was a math test I wasn't ready for, and by Thursday it felt stupid to walk back in like nothing happened. We went to the park and then the diner by the pharmacy and sat there until last bell. That's it; nobody dragged me anywhere, and nothing happened beyond me making it worse twice.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: All right. You're grounded from going out with Mara for a while, and tonight we're calling the counselor together and figuring out how you fix the classes you missed. Next time something starts sliding, you bring it to me before it turns into two afternoons and a borrowed phone.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Look at that, I found the last two coffees before the lunch rush wiped the place out. One for me, one for the person glaring at spreadsheets all week. Mind if I grab this chair?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You really did not need to do that. I can get my own coffee. Go ahead and sit if you want.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That sounded more ceremonial than a coffee handoff usually deserves. It is not a hostage situation, Harper. Just take it before someone from finance swoops in.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I said I can get my own coffee. Please do not bring me things without asking. It is not helpful.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Okay, wow. I was not trying to launch a campaign here. It is a cup with a lid, not a binding contract.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Then do not turn it into a joke when I am being clear. I asked people not to do this kind of thing for me. That includes coffee.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: People? So this is some general policy now? Because from where I am sitting, it sounds a lot like my name got attached to it the second I walked over.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: This is not about you buying coffee. I asked people not to do this for me because I do not like feeling handled.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I thought you were mad at me from the meetings; I brought it because I was trying to smooth that over. That joke landed a lot worse than I expected.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: The meetings were the meetings. This hit a different nerve. If I snapped, that was about the pattern, not a scorecard with your name on it.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: All right. I missed the memo, and then I walked straight into it with extra foam. That is on me.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You were not the only one who missed it; I only mentioned it a couple of times last week. I just need people to let me handle my own basics. It keeps things simpler.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Simple I can do. No surprise coffee, no mystery muffin, no dramatic chair-pulling entrance. I can retire the whole cafeteria bit.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You do not need to avoid the table. Just ask first, and skip the assumption that I will want the gesture because it is friendly. Those are different things.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Fair enough. Next time I will use words before caffeine. And for the record, finance is still not getting this one.

messages.speaker: Harper
