messages.text: But the point is to get people moving, not wait until every line item has a seal on it. If neighbors show up, volunteer, talk to each other, that changes things too. So you'll support it, right, if it's doing that much at least?

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: You're asking for a yes as if that's a receipt stamp. A crowd gathering around a banner can mean a lot of different things, and not all of them are useful. Why is the public part carrying so much weight for you?

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Because people keep saying they care and then nothing leaves the group chat. This would put faces out here, not just comments online. So you'll support it, right, instead of standing back and picking at it?

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: There it is. If I don't nod along, suddenly I'm the one standing in the way. I'm not interested in being marched into a decision because a flyer looks cheerful next to a coffee cup.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: And I'm not talking about a flyer like it's sacred. I'm talking about a chance for the block to look less worn down and less disconnected. You keep answering like the only respectable move is to hold everything at arm's length.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Holding it at arm's length keeps a person from signing onto nonsense. If this money could do more through smaller repairs, school supplies, or direct aid, a stage and paint might be the flashy version of helping, not the best one. That's the part you're skimming past.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Maybe I am reacting to how public and uplifting it feels. Maybe that part lands harder on me than the boring details on the bottom.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: And maybe I am dismissing it because I only trust what can be measured. That still leaves the question of whether this plan earns support, but it's a different argument than the one we were having a minute ago.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Fair enough. If the organizers could show where the money goes and what the event is supposed to change besides the mood for a day, that would help. I don't need it to be flawless, but I can ask better questions than "does it look inspiring."

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: That would make it easier to take seriously. If the public event brings people in and the funds are actually tracked, then the visible part and the practical part don't have to compete. I'd rather see both than choose one on faith.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Then maybe we don't have to treat this like a yes-or-no loyalty test. We could check who is running it and whether they have a budget before writing it off or waving it through. If it holds up, you'll have fewer reasons to glare at the flyer, and I'll have better reasons to hand it to people.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: You packed the blue bag. That's usually the one with the charger in the side pocket. If you're taking it, move the album before it slides off the table.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: I'm going tonight, and I'm not arguing about it. The album can stay where it is.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I didn't say you were arguing. I'm folding towels, not blocking the door. Just don't leave the lamp on again.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Good, because I don't need permission to stay somewhere else for one night. You can keep folding and doing that quiet thing if you want.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: You always call it a thing when I'm not filling the room for no reason. One night is one night. Did you feed the plant by the window?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: See, that's exactly it. You skip over the part that matters and toss out something tiny like the plant, like this is just me misplacing my keys.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: What part are you waiting for? A checklist? You packed a bag, you're leaving, and you'll probably be back tomorrow.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Probably? That's nice. You make it sound like I'm drifting out to sea because I grabbed a toothbrush and a sweatshirt.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: That's not what I said. You're the one turning an overnight bag into a courtroom exhibit.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Because you're sitting there like you've already got a verdict and you're waiting for me to fill in the blanks. You don't have to say anything out loud for it to land.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Then stop trying the case in your head and say whatever you're trying not to say. Or don't. Either way, the couch will still be covered in laundry when you get back.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: There it is. You want me to put it in neat little sentences so you can decide whether it counts. You do not get to make me explain this.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I already know your sister asked you to stay with her tonight. I saw the preview when your phone lit up on the counter.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: You what? So this whole time you knew, and you sat there acting like I was making a scene over nothing.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I didn't pick up your phone. It flashed, her name was there, and the first line was enough. I wasn't trying to make you say it.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Then maybe don't keep that in your pocket while I'm standing here wondering why you're looking at me like that. You could've said, 'Go help her,' and this would've been over.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: And then I'd be saying I read something that wasn't offered. That wasn't going to land well either. I kept it neutral and that clearly went great.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Neutral isn't what that was. It felt slippery. Next time my family is having a rough night, I don't want to stand in my own living room feeling screened.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: You're right about that part. I should've said I saw enough to know it wasn't about us and left the rest alone. I can feed the plant and shut off the lamp.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Take care of the plant, lock up, and don't touch my phone again, even by accident. I'll call when I know how late it'll be.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You grabbed the window table before the whole floor got claimed. Nice. Do we have enough room, or are these library books about to take over?

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: They're fine there. Let me just spread this out. The handout's weirdly specific, so can we figure out exactly what we're missing first?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Sure. You've already got the laptop open like this is an emergency. What are you seeing?

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Theory section, case example, outside source, citations. And we need the framework from the book, plus at least one article from the database. I'm just trying to sort what has to come from here and what doesn't.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Okay. So what else do we even need before we can start? Because it sounds like you're building a scavenger hunt.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Not a scavenger hunt. I just don't want to get halfway in and realize we're missing something obvious. If we list it now, it'll go faster.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Right. How do you want to do this, then? Divide up books first, or talk through the topic before you make more little piles?

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Books first. If we don't have the theory source, then talking through the topic won't help much. We should also check whether the article has to be peer-reviewed before we start pulling random things.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You say "we" and then keep answering your own questions. It's kind of impressive, actually. What are you thinking besides source triage?

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: I'm thinking the instructions are messy and I don't want to waste our afternoon. The example topics are broad, so the sources matter first. Did you find anything useful yet, or are we still at square one?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: That's a pretty specific way to ask that. I brought my notebook, at least, which is apparently less glamorous than your source triage. Anything else on the sacred list?

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: We need the theory book, one solid article, and whatever notes connect the case to the framework. That's basically it. I'm not trying to make this dramatic; I just want to know what we're missing.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You keep saying that like I'm hiding empty hands under the table. I asked what you needed, and you keep talking around me. So what else is there besides the book and the article?

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Maybe nothing else, depending on what we actually have. That's why I'm asking. If we still need to go hunt things down, I'd rather know now than in forty minutes.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You keep acting like we're missing half the materials. And every time I ask, you tighten everything back into a checklist.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: I already heard back from the professor that we only need one article, and I thought you didn't have anything yet. That's why I was trying to pin down the list instead of wandering around with five tabs open.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I actually checked out the theory book already; I was waiting to see if you'd ask me for it. It's in my backpack. So maybe we weren't missing half the materials after all.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You had it the whole time? Wow. Okay, that makes this a lot easier, and also makes me look a little ridiculous with my categories.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: A little. But less ridiculous now that the mystery has an explanation. Here, take it, and next time maybe start with the professor email before reorganizing the entire table.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Fair. Next time maybe start with the book before making me interrogate a handout. Now we've got the book, one article, and a quieter afternoon than this was heading toward.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: You picked the one open stool in the whole place and it happened to be next to me. That a coincidence, or am I supposed to call this a real date over bar fries and a busted speaker?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: If you call this a real date, this bar needs better lighting. I just had a drink in my hand and saw a spot before somebody else grabbed it.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: That's not a no. You even brought your nice jacket out for a Tuesday, so now I'm suspicious.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: This jacket's clean, that's all it has going for it. You always jump straight to the headline before reading the first sentence?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Only when somebody slides in smiling like that. You could've stayed at the other end with the pool table crowd, but here you are leaning into my ear.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: That's because the music's doing its best to ruin conversation for everyone equally. And the pool table crowd looks like they'd fight over a cue ball.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: So you chose the safer option with me. I can live with that for at least one drink.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: One drink is a very manageable contract. After that I start charging for my company.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: See, that's exactly the kind of line people use when they want the other person to keep going. Should I ask better questions, then? Like whether you planned this.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Planned is generous. This place is close, the bartender pours heavy, and you looked less boring than the TV over the bar.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Less boring than sports highlights is not exactly poetry, but I'll take it. Though every time the door opens, you look over there first.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Everybody looks when the cold air hits. Half the room turns their head every two minutes in here.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Not like that. You've been checking the mirror behind the bottles too, like it owes you an answer.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: You notice a lot. Maybe you're the one taking this place too seriously.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Maybe. Or maybe I'm trying not to be the last person to get the joke.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: There's no joke. We're having a drink and talking, that's all pretty standard bar behavior.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: You keep looking around like you're waiting for someone, so are you actually here with me or not?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Not like that, no. I came over because I saw you and it was easy, but I am waiting on somebody to show up. I should've said that sooner.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Right. Okay, that would've been useful about fifteen minutes ago. Thanks for clearing it up.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Yeah. Sorry. I wasn't trying to make you stand in for something else; I just didn't want to make it weird the second I sat down.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: The printer's finally done, so let's use the quiet before people come back. I was updating the whiteboard, and the deadlines are already tighter than they looked yesterday. If we're deciding anything today, materials need an answer first.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Can we lock down the room first? I brought the notes and the laptop so we can settle the work session in one pass. If we can get the room earlier, the rest should be manageable.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Earlier than two? That's a strange place to start when the supply list is still bloated. The board still shows too many things sitting in the maybe column.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: The maybe column can wait a minute. The room affects who can even show up with enough time to review the draft. I don't want us standing in the hallway with poster pieces again.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: And I don't want another cart full of things ordered before the numbers make sense. You glanced at the total as soon as you walked in, so let's not pretend this is separate. Why are you pushing the room issue before we address costs?

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Because the time matters right now, and I'm not talking about another cart. I just need us to stop treating the room like it's flexible. If we miss the slot, the whole afternoon gets messy.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: The room has been at two on this board all week. What's not flexible is paying for extras when the plan keeps expanding by one small thing at a time. Start with what absolutely has to be bought.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I haven't even opened the materials sheet yet. You're crossing out foam core while I'm trying to talk about when people can be in the same place. Those aren't the same problem.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: They become the same problem when one conversation gets used to open the other. You show up with a folder, a laptop, and a new room request, and then 'the rest should be manageable' somehow appears afterward. That's usually the preface to spending money we don't need to spend.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: You're reading way past what I said. I was trying to keep this from turning into a whole thing before we had the time pinned down. Two o'clock isn't available the way it looks up there.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Then say that plainly instead of circling it. Every time I ask about costs, you jump back to the room, which makes it sound like you're lining up cover for something else. The board is there so we don't make guesses.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I am not asking for more supplies; facilities already told me the meeting room is booked from two to three. That's why I keep saying earlier. I was trying to move it without making it sound like I was dropping a problem on your desk.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Then you should know the budget board is outdated too, because we only have forty dollars left after the reimbursement was denied. That's why I kept stopping at materials. I've been working off a different number than the one behind me.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Forty? Okay, that explains the foam core funeral. If the room's gone at two and the budget's basically lunch money, then we should switch the session to one and use whatever's already in the supply cabinet.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: One o'clock could work if we send the change before noon and keep the agenda tight. We can trim the display plan to printed handouts, tape, and whatever markers the office already has. I'll rewrite the board so nobody keeps pointing at the old total.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I'll draft the room update and the stripped-down materials list, then bring it back before you erase anything important. We can cut the sample mounts and keep the comparison chart on the laptop. That should keep the meeting useful without turning this into another scavenger hunt.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Let's just go with the leaner version and move. That checklist's already tight enough, and the laptop draft matches it.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: I want to compare both versions before we decide. The notes are split out here for a reason, and the longer workflow covers the review pass more cleanly.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: You already did the sorting part. We don't need to spend forever on this when the shorter path still gets the main work done.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Can we walk through the pros and cons one more time before we lock anything in? This version gives us room to do it properly, especially at the end.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: The end is exactly where we can trim. The extra formatting pass is nice, but it doesn't change the analysis.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: It changes how the whole thing lands, though. If we're sending something under our names, I'd rather not make it look rushed when we still have space to do it right.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: You're treating the polish step like it's the backbone. We need the numbers, the comparison table, and a clear summary; the rest can stop being precious.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: That's not what I'm saying. I'm asking why you're pushing this so hard when the difference is basically one extra pass and a little cleanup.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Because one extra pass turns into three once we start tweaking language and spacing. You know how this goes when we leave the pages spread all over the break table and keep reopening decisions.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Why are you acting like we have to lock this down today? Yesterday this wasn't some emergency.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Because the manager moved the deadline up by two days this morning. We can still keep the core analysis if we cut the extra formatting pass. Look, it's right here in the email.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: You could have started with that. Okay, then the longer workflow doesn't fit anymore; let's keep the comparison table and drop the second polish round.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Fine. Core analysis, summary, table, done; no decorative cleanup marathon. If you handle the comparison notes, I'll tighten the draft on the laptop and strip out the duplicate formatting tasks.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: That works. I'll mark which comments are essential on the printouts so we don't keep circling the same edits, and I'll leave the visual tweaks for last if there's any room.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Perfect. Once you've flagged those, roll them over here and I'll merge them before lunch so we're not chasing this tonight.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Deal. I'll stop building two parallel versions and just turn these notes into one clean set for the draft.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: The wipers are losing that fight. You always wait too long to change them. The whole windshield sounds like it's being scrubbed with a rake.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Adds character. Besides, we're almost there unless every light on this road has a personal issue with me. This one definitely does.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You've hit three in a row, so maybe. It's warm in here, though. Dashboard makes it look like we're driving a submarine.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: A very cheap submarine with a coffee stain and a check engine light. So— actually, never mind, green now. Can you see if that gas station on the corner is still open?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: It is. Sign's flickering, which feels encouraging somehow. You can keep going if you want.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I'm good. Just thinking out loud. Rain makes everyone weird and philosophical for no reason.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Some people were already weird before the rain helped. You keep doing that thing with the steering wheel. If you're late for something, just say that.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I'm not late. I mean, not exactly. Just trying to pick a decent stretch of road where neither of us gets rear-ended during an awkward sentence.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: That's a promising description. If this is about Mom asking whether you'll come by Sunday, I already told her she'd survive a week without taking attendance. You don't need to rehearse a defense.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Good to know you've appointed yourself counsel for the accused. It isn't Sunday. It's just— you've been quiet, and every time I start talking you look like you're about to object.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: I wasn't preparing a cross-examination. I just didn't want to interrupt whatever spreadsheet is running behind your eyes. It can wait if you're sorting something out.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: That's the problem with you, you say things like that and make me sound like I schedule my own weather. I'm sorting something out, yes. But if you were about to say something, say it.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: It wasn't polished yet. And this doesn't seem like a polished-car-ride kind of night anyway. Go ahead, since you've been circling it for the last ten minutes.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Fine. I took the job in Portland, and I leave in three weeks. I was trying to find a version of that sentence that didn't sound like I was dropping a cinder block in your lap.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Three weeks. You already took it. That's why you've been doing all this traffic-light theater.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Yeah. Marlowe— hold on. What's with the phone? You've been gripping it like it's going to go somewhere if you let go.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: I almost called you this afternoon from the pharmacy parking lot and then sat there until it got dark. I haven't really been sleeping, and today I forgot where I put the car after I paid for groceries. I kept thinking if I picked the right moment, it would come out less dramatic.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Hey. Okay, forget how I said it, forget Portland for one minute. How long has that been going on, and why were you sitting with it by yourself?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Long enough that the pharmacist started using my first name like we're friends. Not long enough that anyone else has noticed, apparently. I didn't want to hand you a mess and then find out you were packing boxes.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: You don't have to package this neatly for me. Three weeks is three weeks, not disappearing, and tonight is still tonight. Tell me what happened at the pharmacy, and then we'll figure out who you're seeing tomorrow and how I'm in it after that.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Okay, ignore the espresso machine screaming behind me for one second. My landlord slipped that under the door this morning, and I've been carrying it around all day. The bigger unit upstairs opened up.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You brought paperwork to coffee? That's serious. What's the catch?

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: The rent jumps, but not by as much as I expected. And it's got the extra closet, actual light in the bedroom, and I wouldn't have to keep storing half my life in your car trunk after weekends. I need another set of eyes before I answer.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: How much of a jump? And is it the same lease length?

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Twelve months either way. The bigger place is four hundred more, which sounds bad until you look at what I'm already paying for the tiny one and how cramped it gets. If I sign this place, we'd finally have enough room.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Enough room for what, exactly? Just less tripping over boxes, or are you doing a whole spreadsheet future thing over there?

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Both, maybe. You keep leaving sweaters and chargers at my place anyway, so the universe is already halfway there. And the commute would still be easy for me, so this is really about whether the extra space makes sense.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: When do they need your answer? This week?

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Yeah, by Friday. That's why I'm talking fast and waving receipts at you in public like a cartoon. Can you help me decide today?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Today is a big ask. Have you looked at what the total is after utilities and the parking fee?

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: I did, and it still works if I'm not reckless. Plus upstairs means no neighbor practicing drums under the floor at midnight. I'm not trying to make this weird; I just don't want to pick blind on something this big.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Right. No, I know. It's just a lot to lay out between iced coffee and that guy grinding beans like he's angry at them.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Then let's make it simple. Bigger place, more rent, better light, better storage, less balancing your overnight bag on a dining chair. That's the pitch.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Parker—

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: And if I pass, it's another year in the shoebox. So when I point at this receipt and say my landlord needs an answer this week about the bigger place, I kind of need more than your eyebrows. What do you think?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I can't help choose that because I already took the Seattle job and I haven't told you yet. It starts in two months.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: You already took it. So this whole time I've been talking about leases and closets, and you were sitting there with that in your pocket? Since when?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: The offer came through last week, and I signed two days ago. I kept trying to find a better way to say it than dropping it on you between cold brew and a muffin display. Then you put that receipt on the table and I waited too long.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Last week is not nothing. You asked about the deadline like we were sorting it out together. Were you ever going to say it before Friday, or was I supposed to hear about Seattle after I signed for an extra bedroom?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You were supposed to hear it from me before any lease got signed, and not like this. I should've said it the second you started talking about upstairs. Ask whatever you need to ask, and I'll answer straight.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: Look at what they said. Just read that part again. My coffee's been sitting here for ten minutes and I still can't even touch it.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Okay, let me see. It could mean a lot of things, Peyton. The line itself is pretty short, and with all this noise in here it's probably not helping either.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: You're doing that careful voice. I asked what you think it means, not what it could possibly mean in some abstract universe. People don't write like that when everything's fine.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I'm not doing a voice. I'm saying this doesn't automatically mean they're upset with you. Some people send clipped replies when they're rushed or already juggling too much.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: Right, so we're starting with excuses for them. Great. I hand you my phone and somehow I'm the one on trial across a sticky coffee shop table.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: No one's putting you on trial. I'm looking at the wording because you asked me to. If I thought it was obvious, I'd say that.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: You keep pointing at the screen like the whole story lives in those two lines. It doesn't land out of nowhere. That's why this feels so bad.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Then tell me the rest of it. So far you've only shown me this reply and asked what it means. From just this, I don't read a door slamming shut.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: Because if I start with the rest, it sounds pathetic. And if you already think this is me making something huge out of nothing, there's not much point, is there?

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I didn't say that. I'm trying to keep you from pinning everything on one blunt message. That's different from saying nothing happened.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: It doesn't feel very different from this side. You saw it, you paused, and then you went straight into all the reasons they might deserve the benefit of the doubt. You didn't even ask what happened before.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Fine, what happened before? I'm asking now. Start wherever makes this make more sense than just those two lines.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: I already double-texted before this, so if you think I made it weird just say it. There, happy? That's the part I didn't exactly want to lead with while that grinder is screaming behind us.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Wait, I didn't know that. I thought you were only reacting to this one message. That changes why it hit you, not into some proof that you ruined everything.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: I sent one check-in, then another a while later because the first one sat there. Then this comes back all clipped like that. So now every word on my screen feels ten times louder.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Okay, now I get why you're stuck on it. Two follow-ups don't make you impossible to deal with, and this still sounds like them more than some final verdict on you. I've seen them text like a robot when their day is upside down.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: You could've said that earlier. I was sitting here thinking you were about to tell me I practically chased them into the street. That's why I kept pushing.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I would've asked different questions if I'd known there were extra texts hanging over this. I wasn't trying to line up evidence against you. I just thought you wanted help reading one message.

messages.speaker: Peyton
messages.text: I wanted you to tell me I didn't make a complete mess of it. Or at least that this doesn't automatically mean they saw my name pop up and groaned. Hearing the other part helps more now.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: You didn't make a complete mess of it. A couple follow-ups after waiting isn't some grand disaster, and that reply still has plenty of room in it. Finish your coffee before it turns to sludge, and if they answer later with actual warmth, you owe me half your muffin.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Can we start with this highlighted line before everyone gets in here? The room on Thursday at four, the one in Conference C. What's the status on that slot?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: We should look at the whole schedule first. That room touches the workshop flow, the panel timing, and the setup crew, so it isn't just one line by itself. The budget sheets are right there.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I saw the budget sheets. I'm asking about access, not the catering numbers. Is that room available to us or not?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: There's still some process to sort out. I don't want to box us into one option before we check what the rest of the afternoon looks like. We have other spaces on the list.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: The other spaces don't match the equipment layout, and you know that. You kept this folder separate for a reason, so what's actually in there? If it's just a request form, open it.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: It's the booking correspondence and a few notes, nothing dramatic. I'd rather not spread half-finished paperwork all over the table two minutes before the meeting starts. Let's keep this organized.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Organized is fine, but vague isn't helping. Every time I ask about that room, you slide over to some other page. If there's a snag, say the snag.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: I'm saying the schedule has to hold together, not just one booking. If we grab something too early and then need to change it, that creates a mess for everyone. I'd rather avoid that kind of scramble.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You keep talking like this can wait until after the meeting. It can't all be 'let's circle back' every time something useful comes up. I need a straight answer on whether that slot is being held.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Held is a strong word. It's in discussion, and there are still pieces around staffing and priority use. That's why I'm not putting a big check mark next to it yet.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: The coordinator told me that slot is still open only if you confirm it before this meeting starts, so are you actually protecting it or keeping me out of it?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: You talked to the coordinator already? Then you know this isn't just me sitting on it for fun. I was trying not to lock us into something before we had the full picture.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: What I know is that the clock was real, and you left that part out while telling me to compare spreadsheets. That makes this look less like caution and more like gatekeeping. If the slot matters to the plan, say yes and we can sort the rest after.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: I left it out because the way these things get used later lands back on me when the room, staffing, and complaints don't line up. You dropping a deadline on the table at the last second doesn't make that disappear. But I'm not saying no.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Then don't make me pry every detail out of you when it's something both of us are working around. Confirm it now, and put my name on the follow-up so this doesn't keep running through one person. We can walk into the meeting with that settled.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Fine, I'll send the confirmation before they start. After that, the follow-up goes on both of our inboxes, and the setup questions get handled in the open. Next time, don't wait until the last minute to show me what you've already heard.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: I need your honest advice before I decide what to do with this. Ignore the noise for a second—look at this section here. This is the part they need to focus on.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Okay. So you're deciding whether this is too risky to push through? The line's practically at our table, so give me the short version while I read.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: We pitch on Friday, and if this lands, the pilot gets real funding instead of another six months of stalling. Everyone else is making louder promises with less substance. I'm trying not to lose on presentation.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: That is a big jump. You highlighted forty-eight percent growth like it's the hinge for the whole thing. Where did that increase come from?

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: From the pilot trendline, mostly. Once they see momentum, the rest of the proposal makes sense. If the headline lands, they'll actually read the operational plan.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Can you walk me through how this number connects to the appendix? I'm seeing a different set of figures back here. Maybe I'm following the wrong column.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: The appendix is too granular for the board anyway. They don't sit there reconciling every table; they look for whether the case is strong enough to back. The point is whether the project deserves room to work.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Maybe. But if the front page says one thing and the back pages say another, that's usually where people start asking questions. Why does this growth figure not match the appendix?

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Keep your voice down. I swapped in the projected pilot numbers so the board would take it seriously; the real results were much weaker. On paper like this, if you lead with the weak version, it's dead before anyone hears the actual value.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Projected numbers? Phoenix, that's not a stronger headline, that's a different result. If someone checks this against the appendix, they're going to see exactly what happened.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: They would also see a good project that never got a fair shot because the first page didn't sparkle enough. The projection isn't invented out of thin air; it's where the pilot was supposed to go without the rollout delays. I'm not talking about some fake company with fake customers.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Then put the projection where projections belong and leave the results as results. Right now it reads like the pilot already did what you only expect it to do. That's the kind of detail that makes everything else look dirty.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: You make it sound cleaner than the process actually is. Every proposal polishes the edges, especially when the people with the money only reward confidence. If I walk in with the unvarnished version, they pass, and the work dies with it.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Polishing edges isn't the same as switching labels. You're asking a board to trust a document that blurs what happened and what you hope happens next. If the work can stand up, let it stand up without that.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: So your answer is to hand them the weaker packet and watch them fund something flashier and emptier. That's easy advice when you're not the one trying to keep a team alive. The board says it wants rigor, then buys confidence.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Then give them rigor and confidence. Put the actual pilot numbers on the front, add the projection beside them, and explain the gap without pretending it's closed. If they only say yes to the swapped version, that's not really a yes you can use.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: You really think that lands in that room? 'Here are the disappointing results, but trust the trajectory anyway.' They smell weakness in about ten seconds.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Maybe some of them do. But if this goes through as written, the first hard question turns the whole pitch into a problem bigger than weak results. Fix the numbers or don't send it.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Wow, same long table, same flickering lamp. We really do keep picking the most romantic spot in the library. Did you already claim the good outlet?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Look at this version first. It's the file open here, not the one from last week. The headings changed.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Straight to business, huh. I brought the notebook and even showed up on time, so I thought I earned at least one normal greeting. Are we still doing intro and lit review, or are you making me pass a document checkpoint first?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Document checkpoint first. Scroll down to the section list. It'll save us from doing the wrong thing twice.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: You say that like I came here ready to sabotage the whole course. Last time we had a system: I drafted the opening, you cleaned up the parts with actual citations, and somehow it worked. This feels very front-desk clerk of you.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Last time was last week. This draft isn't that draft. Can you just read the updated headings before we split anything?

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: I am reading them. I'm also noticing you're talking to me like we're strangers stuck in a group project. If this is about me bringing a notebook instead of printing fifty pages, you can mock my organizational crimes more creatively.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: It's not about the notebook. It's about getting the structure right before you start writing an introduction that doesn't belong there anymore. That's the issue.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Then why not just say that instead of doing the icy librarian routine? You don't have to act like I'm contaminating the table because I said hi first. I'm sitting here, aren't I?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I'm not freezing you out; the professor updated the draft this morning, and your section is methods now. If you want, I can outline the sources and you can take first pass on that part while I handle the literature review.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Oh. That would have been useful about three minutes ago. Methods, seriously? That's what I get for arriving cheerful.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I was trying to get you to look at the screen. The email came early, and the professor moved the whole middle section around. Methods is heavier, so I'm offering the source map.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Okay, fair enough. Rotate it back a little—there. If you flag the studies they want emphasized, I can build the methods section without pretending I memorized the sample sizes from thin air.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I highlighted three already and put comments in the margin. Use the revised rubric too, because they added that comparison paragraph at the end. We can keep the terminology consistent if you send me your first pass tonight.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Tonight is manageable. And for the record, the front-desk clerk comment can go in the bin next to my very professional notebook entrance. The updated draft does make your tone look slightly less dramatic.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Slightly is generous. I'll send you the professor's email so it doesn't look like I invented a new section to make your life harder. The margin notes should tell you what level of detail they're after.

messages.speaker: Parker
messages.text: Good, because I was absolutely preparing a speech about your suspicious commitment to formality. Send the email, I'll draft methods, and you can stop guarding the laptop like it's classified. We might even survive one table without causing a scene.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: That's the plan. I'll take lit review, you take methods, and we'll merge tomorrow before class. If something in the comments is unclear, ask before you guess.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Can you come sit for a minute, or are the plates suddenly urgent? You've been moving around this kitchen like the faucet has better timing than I do.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: They're done. I just wanted to finish what I started. What is this about?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Do you even notice how different you've been with me lately? Dinner, bed, coffee in the morning, all of it feels like you're somewhere a few rooms over.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I don't think things are as bad as you're making them sound. It's been a busy stretch, that's all.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You say that like I pulled this out of nowhere. I've been sitting at this same table all week watching you answer me in half-lines.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I'm answering you now. Let's not turn this into a whole thing before we even figure out what you're asking.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: What I'm asking is pretty simple. When I talk to you lately, do you hear a person you're still close to, or just another thing that needs replying to?

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: That's not a fair way to put it. You're making it sound like I've been shutting a door in your face.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Then give me a straight answer this time. Because every careful little sentence from you lands like you're trying not to touch any of this.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I'm trying not to make this worse. Every time you come in this serious, it feels like you've already got a verdict and you're waiting for me to sign it.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: If I had a verdict, I wouldn't still be sitting here with cold tea asking the same question. I keep asking because you keep stepping around it.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Because the way you're asking sounds like nothing I say is going to count unless it comes out exactly right. That's hard to walk into.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I am not trying to trap you; I just need to know whether you still let me in. That's all this has been.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: River. That's not a small thing to hear you ask like that. You are not outside; I've just been holding too much with both hands and pretending that looked the same as being here.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: It didn't look the same. It looked like you kept leaving a little early, even when you were standing right there.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I know. I kept telling myself you'd read the difference between quiet and gone, and that was a cheap shortcut. You shouldn't have had to guess from across the table.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I can handle quiet. It's the guessing that wears holes in everything.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Then no more guessing on this part: I still reach for you, even when I make a mess of showing it. Lately I've been packing things away instead of bringing them over, and you've been getting the closed cupboard version of me.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: That helps. Just don't hand me the polished version and call it enough, okay?

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Okay. And if I start doing that again, don't sit here with a cold mug for a week before you drag me back to this table.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Hi, Taylor. You're good now—I can see you. I've got the project outline open, so I'll share my screen and walk through the structure.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Thanks. Sorry, my camera decided to point at the ceiling for a second. Go ahead.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: No problem. So the main thing is the scope is narrower than people first assumed, and from the previous exchange, the comparison section needs to stay pretty short. I drafted a breakdown by section so we don't lose time.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Okay. When you say narrower, are you thinking fewer sources, or a tighter question with the same number of sources?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Tighter question, mostly. The sources can still be solid, but the angle has to stay focused enough that the methods and comparison don't sprawl. That's why I put the document into background, framework, case example, and then a brief comparison at the end.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: That division makes sense. On the comparison part, is the short length because of the page limit, or because that point was already settled somewhere?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Both, basically. There was already some guidance on keeping it concise, and if we stretch that section it starts to look like a different paper. Better to anchor the argument early and use the comparison to support it rather than carry it.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Just to clarify, when you say 'from the previous exchange,' do you mean something sent to me, or was that from another conversation?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: That was from a separate thread, actually—with the professor and Sam. It wasn't sent through to you yet. The note was that the comparison should be present, but not treated like a second main section.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Got it. That helps. If there's anything else from that thread shaping the outline, send it over when you have a chance so I'm working from the same version.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Yes, I'll forward the relevant parts after this. For now, the current version on screen reflects the main constraints: focused question, limited comparison, and clear division of labor. If you take the framework section, I can keep the structure consistent across the draft.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I can do framework. Before I start, which theorists are already in the running there, and which of those came from that thread versus your draft?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: The thread only pushed the overall direction; the names in here are mine for now. I put down Goffman and one media theory source as placeholders, mostly to keep the argument from getting too abstract. We can revise them once you've looked at the fit.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Okay, placeholders are fine. I'll build from the direction that's actually been discussed, then adjust once I see the messages. That should keep citations from drifting.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Good. I'll send the thread, clean up the outline labels, and note what's confirmed versus provisional so nothing gets blurred together. Then if you want, we can do a quick check-in after you've got a page or two.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Works for me. Send whatever is confirmed first, and I'll start there. We can compare notes once the framework section has shape.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: This place got louder since last time. The bartender practically slid these over on the music. At least the drinks made it through the crowd.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: And with style, too. Look at us, somehow getting the two seats with the best people-watching angle in the room. Neighborhood bar drama delivered straight to the stool.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You say that like you came here for a show. I came here for fries and one quiet drink, which was obviously a ridiculous plan.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Come on, she doesn't get to be the headline of our drinks. We can do fries, bad music, and me judging that guy's mustache instead.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You're very committed to assigning headlines tonight. The mustache is at least trying its best. Can we keep the conversation on the safe side of the room?

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Safe side? Wow, now I definitely have to look over there. Is it really that weird seeing old office people out in the wild, or is this one of those stories that got ten times better after you left?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: It's not a story. It's a person having a drink, same as everyone else here. The jukebox is losing a fight with three separate conversations, and somehow that's still less tiring.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Okay, okay. I'm just saying, if that's who I think it is, the room does not suddenly belong to her. She can have a stool and a seltzer and absolutely nothing else.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You are making this bigger than it needs to be. The room belongs to whoever got here early enough to grab seats. Speaking of which, guard the fries when they land.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: I can guard fries and still notice you doing that thing where you hold your glass like it offended you. Did she even see us, or are we spiraling over a side profile and a bad haircut?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Please don't say "we" like I dragged you into anything. And don't start waving in that direction; I know you. I'd rather talk about whether you already picked paint swatches for the bathroom without asking me.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Deflection noted, and rude, because those swatches were excellent. Seriously, though, you don't have to act unbothered for me. I already know she was messy back then.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: There it is. You were not casually looking around; you were circling. Next you'll tell me this is an intervention over one woman buying a drink after work.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: I know that's Dana from your old office, but you really do not need to let her ruin your night.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: That is not why I'm being weird. She asked me last week if I'd be interested in a job opening, and I haven't told you because I don't even know if I want it.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Oh. That's a very different sentence. Is this nearby, or is this one of those listings that comes with packing tape and a new zip code?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Different city. Better pay, at least on paper. There isn't an offer sitting in my inbox or anything dramatic, just a message and a phone call I haven't returned.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: You could've said there was a phone call. I would've retired the whole anti-Dana routine a lot sooner. Do you want to talk through the job itself, or just survive the fact that she happens to be ten feet away?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Both, probably. The job sounds good in the sterile bullet-point way jobs do, and the rest of it gets messy fast. I didn't want to make the apartment start feeling temporary over something that might disappear by Monday.

messages.speaker: Rowan
messages.text: Fair. The apartment can stay exactly as annoying and overfull as ever until there's something real to react to. Start with the bullet points, and I'll keep my eyes off Dana unless she comes over and asks for a character reference.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: So, where is this headed tonight? We've got bad lighting, good music, and you doing that thing with your glass like it owes you money. Feels like the kind of night that shouldn't end with a polite hug at the door.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: You always make a small table sound dramatic. Maybe we should just let the night be the night. The drinks aren't even finished yet.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: That's not a no. And you came all the way across town for one drink and a catch-up? I know you better than that.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Do you? It's been a while. People change cities, playlists, sleep schedules.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Playlists, sure. But you're still here, still letting your knee bump mine, still smiling like you're trying not to. So I'm not reading this as nothing.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: I'm sitting in a crowded bar, Charlie, not sending smoke signals. And you still talk like every silence needs a caption.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Fine, I'll add fewer captions. Just one question, then. Is this one of those slow starts where we stop making everything so heavy and see what happens?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: I don't know. Maybe we should just enjoy tonight without turning it into a blueprint.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: That's cute, but you only say things like that when you're halfway in and trying to look casual. You don't have to make it pretty for me. Just give me something real.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Not everything real fits neatly into one sentence. Sometimes a drink is just a drink, and a song is just loud enough to keep people from saying too much.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: You've been close enough to count my freckles for the last hour, and now you're hiding behind the speakers. That's a little unfair. Unless you're about to tell me I've completely imagined this whole thing.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: I didn't ask you to imagine anything. I asked you here because I wanted to see you. That doesn't automatically make this some return to the old schedule.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Then stop circling it. If you want this too, just say it.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: I am leaving in two weeks, and this is not going anywhere. I wasn't going to do this here, but you kept pushing.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Two weeks? You sat here with me all night and left that out. So all of this was what, one last good scene before you disappear?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: It wasn't meant to be a scene. I should have said it sooner, and I didn't. But I'm saying it now, and I can't turn it into something else just because we're sitting here.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: You came prepared. Two coffees and the good bench, too. Either the park finally upgraded its service or you knew I'd show.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Your order hasn't changed in a hundred years, so it wasn't exactly a risky guess. Sit before one of the runners steals your side. It's nicer under this tree when the path gets busy.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Wow, my side. That's advanced planning. And here I was ready to make a weather joke and escape with dignity.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: You can still do the weather joke if you need it. The leaves are doing a lot, and that kid on the scooter nearly took out a pigeon, so the ambiance is strong. How have you been?

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Alive, opinionated, still underpaid by people who use words like synergy without irony. You? You don't usually send a message that says, 'Can we meet at the park?' and then add a smiley face like it's harmless.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I didn't realize punctuation was going to be entered into evidence. I just thought a public place and caffeine made this less dramatic. Besides, you always did better walking into things if there was a cup involved.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Less dramatic is an interesting target. Usually people say easy or quick. So what made you suddenly nostalgic enough to pre-order me?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Do you ever think about us back then? Not in a scrapbook way. Just whether it was as big as it felt while it was happening.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: That's not a coffee question, Jamie. That's a bench-after-sunset question. But sure, sometimes I do, especially when I pass that Thai place where you used to order for both of us because I never learned the names right.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: You learned the names once and then performed confusion every time because the server laughed. You liked having a bit. I guess I was wondering whether it landed somewhere real for you, or if it just turned into one of your stories.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: If this is you checking whether I can still say nice things on command, I probably can. If this is you circling some other point, your turns are getting suspiciously wide. Did something happen, or are you waiting to see whether I reach across the bench first?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: You always do that, turn everything into a test and then act like you stumbled into the answer by accident. I asked because I wanted to know. You don't have to make it into a scene.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: We're already in a scene. There's a spare coffee, your voice is doing that careful thing, and you've asked me about us before you've mentioned work, family, or anyone's dog. So either you missed me, or you're about to hand me a line with a sharp edge on it.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I didn't ask you here to get back together right now. I got a job in Seattle, and I'm leaving in three weeks. I wanted to tell you myself.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Seattle. Right. So the extra coffee was for what, cushioning? You had all of that lined up before you sent the smiley face.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I found out, then I interviewed, then it all moved fast. Every version of saying it over text looked cheap. I didn't want you hearing it from somebody else six months from now like you were a forwarding address.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: You also didn't mention it until after asking whether I still file us under 'real.' That's a pretty elaborate route to a city announcement. Makes a person wonder what exactly they were brought here to provide.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Maybe because I didn't want it to sound like I was dropping a calendar invite and calling that courtesy. Maybe because I needed to know it wasn't nothing before it turned into luggage and airport maps. You mattered too much for a cold update.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: That's almost worse, you know. Not because of Seattle. Because now I get to sit here with your favorite coffee order in my hand and figure out whether this was goodbye, confession, or collecting proof that the old wiring still works.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: You don't have to make it easier for me. I called because leaving without seeing you would've said something ugly, and I didn't want that to be the last version. If you want distance after this, I won't chase you down the path.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: This table is somehow still too small. I’ve got three books open and they all keep sliding into the assignment sheet. The database article titles are a lot cleaner than these chapter names.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: At least we grabbed the outlet side. Okay, sources list, topic, then outline, and we’re fine. If we sort the pile now, this won’t turn into one of those four-hour library marathons.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: I found one book that actually matches the case study, but the other two might cover background better. The sheet keeps saying scholarly and non-scholarly, so I don’t want to box us in too early. There might be some requirement hidden in the wording.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: We already have two journal articles that fit the topic pretty well. If we keep every maybe-source in play, the pile’s going to decide for us. We need to pick something and move.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: I’m not attached to the pile. I just don’t want the final list to look thin if one of those articles turns out to be only half useful. Maybe we should check a few more first.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: A few more is how people end up with twelve tabs and no draft. These two articles cover the main argument, and that book has the methodology section you pointed out. That seems like enough to start shaping the paper.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Maybe for the argument, sure. But if they want different source types across the whole project, we still need to make sure we’re not missing something obvious. There’s a newspaper archive link here too, and probably a report we could use.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Right, but we can spend the whole afternoon collecting categories instead of evidence. Look, I’m circling these two and setting the rest aside for a second. Let’s just commit to these and start outlining.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: You can circle them. I just haven’t finished checking whether the other book is stronger. If we build the outline around the first things we saw, it could get awkward later.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I’m not saying first things only. I’m saying we need an actual plan instead of rotating through every shelf keyword in the catalog. Otherwise we’re going to keep doing this exact part until the library closes.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Okay, then let’s use the sheet and go line by line. The top says analysis, then source integration, then citation format. Wait—down here in the note under required materials, it says three relevant scholarly sources and one supporting non-scholarly source.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Oh, wow. So it doesn’t say we need one of every possible type, just three scholarly that actually fit and one non-scholarly support piece. That changes a lot.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Yeah, that’s much narrower than what we were doing. Then we don’t need the giant pile, just the ones that actually pull weight. The book with the case study probably matters more than the random background one.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: That makes way more sense. Okay, new plan: we keep the two strongest journal articles, you compare the case-study book against the methodology one, and I’ll find one non-scholarly source that supports the context without being flimsy.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: That works. And if the case-study book overlaps too much with the articles, I’ll swap it for something with stronger evidence instead of just adding more. We can stop treating the source list like a scavenger hunt.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Exactly. Relevance over variety, apparently, which would’ve been nice to notice twenty minutes ago. I’ll search for a good report or news analysis while you check which scholarly source gives us the cleanest support.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: I found a chapter in this book that directly addresses the same population as our topic, so that probably beats the broader overview. If your non-scholarly source handles recent context, the rest can stay focused. This suddenly looks much more normal.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Great, then we’ve got a lane. Send me that chapter title, and I’ll drop the articles and the outside source into a shared doc. After that, outlining should finally be the easy part.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: The tea's cold. You made it and then just left it there like none of this could wait five minutes. How long were you going to keep me out of this?

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: I do not know what 'this' is supposed to mean. You have been sitting here staring at your phone and crying, and you have not actually said it. Start at the beginning.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Don't do that clipped voice with me. We're in the same apartment, ten feet apart, and somehow I still get treated like the last person in the room to know anything important. Is that how this works now?

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: If you want an answer, ask a clear question. Vague accusations are not a method. And no, living together does not mean every private matter becomes a household bulletin.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Private matter. Right. So I was just supposed to find out after you left? Maybe from an empty bedroom and a forwarding address.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: That is an impressive leap. Nothing has happened here except you deciding I have apparently committed some unnamed offense. Say what you are talking about.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Was this already decided without me? Just answer that one part. For once, don't make me drag every word out of you.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: You do not need every detail the moment I hear something. That does not make it a conspiracy. It means I get to think before the entire room starts reacting.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: So there is something. And you were going to sort it all out neatly and hand me the finished version when it was too late to say anything. That's generous.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: This is exactly why I wait until there is something concrete. You turn one partial piece into a verdict and then put me on trial in the living room. Not every independent decision is a betrayal.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Don't flatten this into one of your speeches about independence. I am talking about being shut outside the door while you pack up the whole house in your head. You make it sound like there's no place for anyone else in the process.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: No, you are making it sound like I need permission to consider my own life. Those are not the same thing. If this is your way of pushing me to drop it before I have even sorted through it, that is not happening.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I saw the message about the transfer on your phone. There, now it has a name. So stop standing there like this came out of nowhere.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: You went through my phone? Sutton, that was an offer, not a signed lease or a moving truck. And if you had started with that, we would not have spent the last ten minutes talking past each other.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: It was open, and your face changed when it lit up. After that, you barely said two words all evening. Tell me this much: was I going to hear about it before boxes showed up, or after?

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Before boxes. Before any decision, actually, once I knew whether there was even a decision to make. I had one message from work and half a cup of tea, not some secret escape plan.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Then don't leave me piecing things together from a screen and a shut door. Big things land in this apartment and suddenly everything goes quiet, and I'm supposed to act like that means nothing. Next time, say it while it's still messy.

messages.speaker: Cameron
messages.text: Next time, you ask me directly instead of reading over my shoulder. I can say something earlier than I usually would, and you can give me room to think without writing the ending first. That is a far better arrangement than this.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I turned the screen so you could see the chart without coming around the table. The gap is right there in the fourth quarter, and if we keep pretending it will smooth itself out, the committee will ask why nobody acted. We should send the recommendation today.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I'm looking at it. I just want to walk through the assumptions line by line before anything goes out. Once we put our name on the harshest option, it won't come back quietly.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: There isn't a softer interpretation hidden in the formatting. Revenue came in low, reserves are already spoken for, and two hundred thousand is still missing. Delaying the recommendation doesn't change the arithmetic.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Start with reserves, then. Your printed summary says one thing, and the chart on the laptop folds in another category at the bottom. I'm trying to see why those belong together.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Because they're both unavailable for operating relief, which is the only category that matters for this vote. You're doing that thing where every figure gets reopened until the deadline passes. The board won't reward hesitation.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Careful isn't the same as evasive. If we're asking people to absorb cuts, I need more than a slide and a deadline. Show me where the two hundred thousand becomes unavoidable rather than convenient.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Convenient? That's not fair. I've been rebuilding this model since last week because nobody else wanted to put the ugly version on the table, and the ugly version is still the responsible one. We can stop circling and make the recommendation now, or let the committee discover we're unwilling to say what the numbers say.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I didn't say nobody should say hard things. I'm asking why this page treats the shortfall as fixed when some of these notes suggest movement this morning. You keep pointing to the chart as if it settled every question before the room even filled.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Because the chart is built from the finance packet everyone received. If something truly changed, it would be in writing, not floating around as hopeful talk five minutes before a vote. Right now what I have in front of me is still a hole that has to be covered.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Not everything arrives in the packet on the same schedule. That's why I brought the folder instead of relying on the summary email. Will you go back to the assumption under donor restrictions?

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Restricted money can't patch an unrestricted operations problem unless the restriction matches exactly, and usually it doesn't. That's why I said reserves don't help and why the cut remains the cleanest option. If you're holding out for an exception, that's a thin basis for a recommendation.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I'm holding out for accuracy. The way you're presenting it, there's one road and everyone else is simply too squeamish to take it. That's not a great habit in this room.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: And the habit of asking for one more pass, one more clarification, one more sheet from the folder isn't helping either. At some point someone has to say no to the comfortable story. The numbers leave no room for us to act as though this can be avoided.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Your chart still assumes the missing two hundred thousand, but the chair confirmed this morning that it was covered by a restricted donor gift. Here—read the signed note. That's why I kept asking about your assumptions.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Let me see that. This wasn't in the packet, and nobody copied me on any update from the chair. If the restriction is written this narrowly, then the immediate gap isn't what this model shows.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Exactly. So the cut you're urging isn't the only responsible option in front of us. We can talk about staffing, timing, and contingency planning without treating today's vote like an emergency amputation.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I said the immediate gap isn't there, not that the underlying trend vanished. The donor gift covers this hole, but it doesn't repair the pattern that created it. We still need something stronger than crossing our fingers and thanking the chair.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Then let's write it that way. No immediate cut tied to a shortfall that no longer exists, but a revised recommendation on longer-term risk and what to monitor next quarter. That would be easier to defend, and harder for anyone to say we rushed past the facts.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I brought the library books before someone else grabbed the good ones. Your mug's still too hot, so don't knock it into the notes. The assignment sheet says ten pages, which is more manageable if we keep the structure clean.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You say that like I've never survived a table full of paper before. Look, if we split sources now, we could finish early and make this better than just manageable. There's room to do something a little more original with the case study section.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Original can turn into messy fast. I'd rather we answer exactly what they're asking and make it polished. We can each take two articles, then build a plain outline from the prompt.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Plain isn't always polished. We could make ours stand out if I take the lead on the final write-up and tie the sources together instead of doing the standard compare-and-contrast thing. It'd read smoother that way.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Let's not get too elaborate. The compare-and-contrast is on the sheet for a reason, and this angle you wrote in the margin is probably more trouble than it's worth. Why don't you handle gathering examples and I'll shape the outline so we don't drift.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Examples and that's it? You moved the paper over like I was about to write in crayon. If the issue is the draft, I can do the draft and the presentation too.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: That's exactly what I'm trying to avoid, one person grabbing all the visible parts. We don't need a performance piece; we need something solid that doesn't invite extra questions. Shared notes, shared edits, simple presentation.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You keep saying simple like it's the only safe word in the language. Every time I bring up anything stronger, you shave it down and hand me a smaller task. It's starting to feel weird.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I'm shaving down risk, not your part. There's a difference. If we stay close to the prompt, nobody has to defend why we got clever instead of clear.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Who's talking about clever for the sake of it? I just don't get why the outline, the framing, the final wording all have to stay in your lane. Usually when you do that, there's a reason you could just say.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Usually when someone volunteers for draft and presentation before we've even divided the reading, there's a reason for that too. Tapping the rubric and talking about standing out doesn't exactly sound casual. I'm trying to keep this from becoming a showcase.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You keep shutting down every idea like you don't trust me.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: It isn't about trust. The professor is my aunt, and if our project looks showy she'll read it extra critically, so I've been trying to keep it safe without saying why. I should've said it sooner.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Oh. That explains a lot more than 'stay close to the prompt' ever did. I thought this was about me overreaching or you not wanting me near the final draft.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: No, it's the opposite problem. If anything looks like special treatment, it gets harsher, not easier. So when you said stand out, all I could hear was a spotlight landing on the title page.

messages.speaker: Hayden
