messages.text: Okay, then let's stop aiming for spotlight and aim for airtight. You can stop guarding the outline like it's classified, and I'll stop trying to test every boundary you set. We can do a strong version of straightforward.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: That sounds fair. Take the source synthesis and draft the middle sections, and I'll do the intro and conclusion so the tone stays even. Then we both go through the final version together before anything gets uploaded.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Deal. And next time you start crossing out my margins like a suspicious editor, give me one sentence more than 'too elaborate.' I work better when I know what game we're actually playing.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Can you even hear me over this place? They've sent three more since we sat down. I turned my phone over and then turned it back because that somehow felt worse.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I can hear you. And yeah, this is obviously a bad idea. Don't text back tonight.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You say that like you're looking at a cracked windshield. They keep apologizing, and it's not like they vanished for six years. What if they've actually changed?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: People always change right when they want something. Look at the thread—nothing for months, then suddenly a late-night check-in, then a 'can we meet.' That's a pattern, not growth.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Maybe. Or maybe they're finally saying things they should've said before. I didn't bring it up just so you could do message forensics on my drink coaster.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I'm not doing forensics. I'm saying if somebody only shows up when it's convenient for them, you don't reward that by being available on command. Leave it unread till tomorrow at least.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Tomorrow isn't really the point. You make it sound like I'm scheduling a dentist appointment. I asked what you would do, not what an efficiency chart would do.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Fine. I wouldn't go meet an ex in a bar after a string of apologies and vague promises. Especially not one who already taught you how this goes.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You keep saying 'this goes' like it's some machine with labeled parts. Maybe I wanted something a little less... procedural from you. Why are you so focused on who I text back?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Because if you keep leaving the door open for your ex, I don't know what I'm supposed to do here. So yeah, I'm focused on it.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Oh. That's different from 'late-night patterns' and 'don't reply tonight.' You could've started there.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I was trying not to make it weird. That clearly worked great. But I'm not talking about this like it's abstract.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: It sounded abstract. Like you were helping me sort receipts. And I was sitting here wondering whether I should stop bringing things to you if that's all it was going to be.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Don't do that. Bring it to me, just maybe don't hand me a phone full of your ex asking for another shot and expect me to sound neutral. I'm not neutral.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I noticed that part eventually. For the record, I wasn't exactly polishing a reunion speech over here. I wanted to know whether this table was just drinks and noise, or something harder to ignore than that.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Then ignore the ex. See what this is without somebody from your past wedged into it. That seems pretty straightforward to me.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Straightforward is not usually your problem. Timing is. But okay, no reply tonight, and probably not tomorrow either.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Good. Then next time we come here, maybe the phone stays in your bag and this stops feeling like a debate. I'd like that better.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Can you hold your tray a second while I move this ketchup? Thanks. I brought that committee folder down because I need another set of eyes before I answer them this afternoon.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Sure. Is this about the operations committee they mentioned last week? You could probably handle it, depending on what they're asking.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: It's not just showing up to meetings. They want someone to chair the scheduling piece, and that means dealing with three departments that already miss deadlines. If I say yes, it's going to land on my desk for months.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: That sounds heavier than they made it sound. Maybe look at whether you'd get any actual authority with it, not just the cleanup work. Can I show you something first?

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: In a second. The answer depends on whether this gives me visibility or just more people dropping things on me. You said "look at authority"—so do you mean take it only if that's in writing?

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Yes, in writing would help. If they want ownership, they should attach something concrete to it. I just... this might be time-sensitive too.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Everything here is time-sensitive at noon. I'm asking because if I push back, I need a clean reason, and if I accept, I need one just as clean. You're halfway in this conversation and halfway somewhere else.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: I'm listening. For the committee, I'd ask who sets the deadlines and who backs you when people ignore them. Then you know whether you're walking into a title or a mess.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That's useful, but you're still doing that thing where you keep looking at the paper under your arm. If lunch is a bad time, say that instead of giving me the abbreviated version.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: It's not lunch. I just don't want to miss the window on something while we're standing here deciding between mustard packets. And I thought your question was more of a quick calibration.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: It's not a mustard-packet question. If I send the wrong reply, I inherit a problem nobody else wants. So no, I wasn't looking for a shrug and a headline.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Okay. Then my headline answer is don't say yes unless they define scope, reporting line, and end date. But I need to tell you this now—the two-bedroom in our building opened up, applications close at three, and I was hoping we'd apply for it together.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Wait. That's what you've been carrying around? The place on the corner side, with the bigger kitchen?

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: The notice was taped by the mailboxes this morning, and I grabbed a copy on the way out. They marked it first-come review, so I didn't want to leave it until tonight and hear someone upstairs already turned it in.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That explains a lot. What's the rent difference, and do they want current pay stubs again? Also, are you talking about moving because the lease timing works, or because you've been done with our shoebox for a while?

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Four hundred more total, according to the sheet, and yes, they want the usual income paperwork. The lease transfer lines up with our renewal month, and it would mean an actual second bedroom instead of your desk living next to the radiator.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Four hundred total is different from four hundred each. That's manageable if we split it the same way and the utility jump isn't ridiculous. Did you already pick up an application packet, or is this just the notice?

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Just the notice, but the office said forms are online too. We could submit the basic application after lunch and deal with attachments before three if you're on board. Your committee email can probably wait twenty minutes if you're sending questions instead of an answer.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That's true. I can reply with questions and buy time, which is more than this apartment gives us. Show me the fine print, and if there's no weird clause about parking or storage, we should do it today.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Here. They listed the square footage, the rent, and the deadline in bold like they're daring people to hesitate. If you're still okay with it after we read through, we can go upstairs after lunch and send everything before the line starts at the office.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: You picked the one bench with full traffic today. Every runner in the city keeps passing us like we're part of the route. Your coffee's gone cold already.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: It's still warm enough. That dog has looped past three times, though. I think he likes your muffin more than he likes his owner.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: He has good instincts. Hey— we need to talk about something important. Nothing dramatic, just... something that shouldn't wait.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Oh. Okay. You've seemed far away this week. Is something wrong?

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Work's been a lot, that's true, but this isn't about forgetting to text back or getting home late. I wanted to explain it properly before it turned into a whole thing. Let me get through it once.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Right. Properly. You don't usually sound like you're presenting quarterly numbers when it's just me.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I'm trying not to say it badly. There's a new branch opening, and my manager asked me to take point on getting it off the ground. It would mean being away for a while.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Away where? And for how long is "a while" when your office says it? Because they have a talent for pretending calendars don't exist.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Six months, maybe a little less if it runs smoothly. Bristol. I know how that sounds, which is why I wanted to talk before you filled in the blanks yourself.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I wasn't filling in blanks. I just... you've been lining things up in your head all week, and I could tell there was a version of this conversation happening without me. I was trying to say something too.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Then say it. If this is about me being buried in work lately, we can sort that out. I don't want you sitting here thinking you're getting edged out by a spreadsheet.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: It's not about spreadsheets. It's just hard to jump in when you sit up like that and start with "we need to talk." That usually doesn't lead anywhere nice.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Harper—

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I got offered a year away for training.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I was about to tell you they want me in Bristol for six months. We may both have to move, so let's figure out how not to lose us. Start with where yours is, and when they need an answer.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Leeds, and they want one by next Friday. I thought this bench was about to become the place we said something awful and then watched joggers go by. If we're doing calendars and train times instead, I can work with that.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Can you explain why you showed me that message first? Standing out here by the path with people walking past, it lands a little sharper than you may have meant it to.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: I'm just showing you what I got. That's all. I didn't think holding up my phone by a bench was going to turn into this whole thing.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: That comes off very differently from how you're saying it now. You showed me a screenshot saying I "weren't available" right after Saturday came up, so you can see why I'd stop there.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Because that's what Jordan said after you weren't available. Look at the timestamp. It came in this morning.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I see the timestamp. I'm asking why that was the first thing you put in front of me instead of just saying Jordan was confused.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Because if I just said that, it would sound like I was making it up or adding my own spin. The screenshot was supposed to show where it came from.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: But you can hear how it sounds, right? Like I'm being handed evidence and expected to answer for it.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: No, I'm trying to show you I wasn't the one saying it. You keep talking like those are my words when they're not.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I'm talking about what happened when you showed it to me, not just who typed it. If someone passes along something blunt without any lead-in, that still says something.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: So what, I was supposed to soften it first and then get accused of twisting it? I showed exactly what I got because I didn't want any of this pinned on me.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Wait, I think I took this as you blaming me. The way you tapped the message and kept repeating that line about me not being available made it sound like that.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: No, I showed you because Jordan thought you changed plans on them, and I didn't know you'd already promised that time to Jordan yesterday. I was missing that part, and you were missing where the wording came from.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Okay. Yesterday I told Jordan I'd keep Saturday afternoon open, so when I saw that screenshot, it read like I was being called flaky to my face.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: I didn't know you'd already settled it with them. If I'd known that, I wouldn't have just shoved my phone at you like that.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: And if you'd said Jordan was mixed up before showing me the text, this probably wouldn't have gone sideways by the dog walkers. Jordan must've forgotten that conversation or crossed it with something else.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Yeah. I made it look like I agreed with the message when I was really trying to show I hadn't written it. That's on me.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: We're okay. Next time, just start with the part that isn't in the screenshot, and I'll start with asking what happened before I jump on the wording.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Deal. And maybe next time we save this kind of thing for somewhere that doesn't have three strollers and a golden retriever as an audience.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Hey. I grabbed that corner table before the lunch crowd took it, and I got you the usual. This place gets loud near the counter.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Oh—thanks. You didn't have to do that. It's kind of nice back here, though; the window makes it feel less cramped.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Figured coffee first was safer than making you stand in line and yell an order over the grinder. How's your day been so far?

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: A little scrambled, honestly. I almost walked past because I wasn't expecting you to already be set up like this.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: I got here early. Traffic was lighter than I thought, so I had time to claim the least sticky table in the room. That's basically a win in a place like this.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: You make it sound tactical. I don't usually think that far ahead. I mostly just show up and hope the chair doesn't wobble.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: That works until you end up balancing a drink with one hand all afternoon. So, what've you been up to lately? Maya said you've had a lot going on.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Yeah, a few things. Some of it is normal busy, and some of it isn't exactly the kind of thing that drops neatly into catch-up conversation.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Doesn't have to be neat. We can let it sit crooked for a minute if that's easier. No deadline from me.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: That's kind of you to say. I wasn't sure how to bring this up, and now that I'm here, every opening sentence sounds strange out loud.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Start in the middle, then. Or start with the part that sounds worst in your head and it'll probably shrink once it's in the air.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Maybe. There's something important, I just... keep circling it first. You seem very calm for someone being handed a mystery package.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: People say all kinds of things over coffee. Calm's useful. Besides, you asked to meet, not to jump off a bridge.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Right. Still, this doesn't feel like random coffee. The table, the drink, the whole... prepared look. It's making me wonder what part of this is actually a surprise.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: You're reading a lot into a cup with oat milk. I know what you order because you always get the same thing when other people pick the cafe. That's not exactly spy-level information.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Why did you already order exactly what I usually get if you didn't know this was a big talk? You don't even know me that well, so this whole polished setup feels off.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: I heard from Maya that you needed to tell me something important, and I didn't want to make it harder. She didn't give details. I thought if the coffee was already here, at least one awkward part would be gone.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: So everyone got a head start except me. That's great. I came in trying to figure out whether to say anything at all, and you were already arranging the lighting.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: It wasn't everyone. It was one message, and I should've said it earlier instead of acting like this was spontaneous. I was trying to keep the floor clear, not build a trap.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Maybe both happened. I'm not walking out, but I'm not doing the full version now either. The short version is that what I needed to say is about me, and I'd rather not have it arrive through Maya before it arrives from me.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Morning. I've got the draft recommendation up on the shared doc, and the main fork is whether we move ahead with Option B for the next rollout. If you look at the second page, I pulled the cost, timeline, and support notes into one place so we can land on one direction.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I see it. You've already got the recommendation section half written. Before we lock wording, we should probably revisit a few assumptions in there.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: The wording's just a frame so we're not starting from a blank page on a Tuesday morning. Your camera keeps freezing for a second, but I can hear you fine. Which assumptions are you looking at?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: The implementation line mostly. The doc makes it sound cleaner than it's likely to be. I just don't want us locking ourselves in too fast.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: We can adjust details, sure, but I still need a real read from you on the direction itself. Is Option B workable enough to recommend, or are you saying no? The team can't do much with 'maybe slow down' on its own.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I'm saying the way it's framed here skips over what happens after launch. If we're basing the choice on this document, then the assumptions under support load and handoff need another pass. Otherwise the clean version on screen is doing a lot of work.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Okay, but I'm still missing whether you're objecting to the option or to my summary of it. Those aren't the same problem. If there's a fixable gap, we can fix the gap.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: They're not separate if the gap changes who ends up carrying it. Support load isn't just a footnote when it lands on the team every day. I'd rather not sign off on a version that only looks efficient from a distance.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I'm not asking for a ceremonial sign-off. I need to leave this call with a recommendation today. If Option B isn't the one, then I need something firmer than circling the assumptions.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: I'm not stalling you—I already ran a pilot on that option, and it created cleanup work we haven't accounted for. The notes are still in my draft, so I hadn't sent them yet. But the extra manual review showed up almost immediately.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Wait, you already tested it? That changes the conversation quite a bit. How much cleanup are we talking about, and where did it hit first?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Mostly at the handoff point where the data comes in uneven. People had to normalize entries by hand before the next step would even run cleanly. The pilot was small, and it still added enough friction that the time savings on paper didn't hold up.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I wish I'd had that before I built this version, but this is exactly what needs to be in the recommendation. Can you walk me through the numbers you do have, even if the notes aren't polished? I'd rather send something grounded than neat.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Yeah. The sample was limited, so I wouldn't present it like a formal study, but the pattern was consistent enough to flag. We can recommend against full rollout as-is, or put conditions around it so the cleanup piece gets solved first.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Let's shape it around conditions. If leadership sees a flat no without an alternative path, they'll just ask us to rerun the same argument this afternoon. What would make Option B usable without dumping the mess back on the team?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Either we narrow the intake format so the messy cases never enter that path, or we add an automated validation step before handoff. If neither of those is ready, then the recommendation should say pilot-only, not team-wide. That's the difference between manageable and everyone cleaning up after it.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That gives us something solid. I'm changing the header from 'Recommend adoption' to 'Recommend conditional pilot expansion,' and under risks I'll add manual cleanup at the handoff stage. Can I cite your pilot as the basis for that, with the note that fuller documentation follows?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Yes, just don't oversell the sample size. Say early pilot evidence showed recurring manual normalization and that broader rollout depends on validation controls. I'll send the draft notes right after this so the wording matches what I actually found.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Good. I'm adding a final bullet that the team should not absorb manual review as a standing workaround. Once your notes come in, I'll attach them and send this up before noon.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: That works. Leave a line for the two gating fixes, and I'll fill in the language so it doesn't read like an abstract risk. If we're sending a direction today, it should reflect what the rollout will actually ask people to do.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: You went quiet all of a sudden. The coffee's getting cold, and half the campus has walked past us already.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: I know. I was just looking at you trying not to juggle your cup and your backpack at the same time. We spend a lot of time together, and I wasn't sure how you saw that.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: How I saw it? I don't know, it depends on the day. Usually it looks like class, notes, deadlines, you reminding me not to leave things until midnight.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Usually, sure. But not always. Lately it's felt like more than comparing readings and fixing each other's outlines.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: You've seemed busy lately. There are a lot of people who want your attention after class. I figured I was one more person in line.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: One more person in line isn't why I'm here now. I asked if you wanted coffee because I wanted this part, not the lecture recap. Did something happen that made this feel different to you?

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Nothing dramatic. You were having a great time with Maren the other day, and after that this started sounding like one of those careful conversations people have before they sort things into categories.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Maren? We were laughing about her presentation imploding because the projector died. That didn't have anything to do with you. And I'm not trying to sort you into a category.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Maybe not on purpose. But when someone starts asking where things stand in that calm voice, it usually isn't heading somewhere fun. So yes, I'm answering carefully.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: You keep answering like I'm putting you on the spot—if you only see me as someone from class, just say that. I'd rather hear it straight than keep guessing.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That's not what I said. You brought me out here, talked around something for ten minutes, and now it sounds like you're the one drawing the line. If this was your polished way of telling me to keep it to assignments and coffee after exams, you could've skipped the scenic route.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: No, that's exactly the opposite of what I was trying to do. I was circling because getting this wrong with you would matter a lot more than being awkward with anyone else. I wasn't working up to less.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Then say it without the survey questions. Because from where I was sitting, it looked like I was about to get thanked for being reliable and then sent back to the safe column. I can handle plain English better than that.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: Plain English, then: I don't ask everyone to sit in the park after class and stay until the sun's almost down. I wanted to know whether asking you to dinner would land badly or not. Not as a study break, and not because you take good notes.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That would have been useful about twenty minutes ago. I wasn't worried about dinner landing badly. I was trying to figure out whether I mattered once there wasn't a syllabus between us.

messages.speaker: Finley
messages.text: You do. Enough that I managed to turn one simple question into a whole mess on a bench with terrible coffee. So—dinner, properly, if you're still willing?

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Can I at least take my backpack off first, or is this that urgent? You called me in here like I missed court.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Just for a minute. Sit down, please. We need to talk for a minute.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I'll stand. If this is another lecture, I'm not doing it right by the front door with my shoes still on.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I'm not trying to corner you. I need you to be honest with me. That's all I'm asking.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: That sentence always means it's not 'all.' It usually means you've already decided what happened and now I get to fill in the blanks.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Then fill in the part I'm missing. You came home, dropped your keys like they weighed fifty pounds, and went straight to your room.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: So I had a bad day. People are allowed to have those without turning the living room into some kind of hearing.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I'm aware of that. But when the school calls and says there was an incident, I don't get to shrug and pretend not to notice.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: There it is. So this is about school deciding everybody's business belongs to everybody else. Great.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Lower your voice and stop swinging at me before I finish a sentence. I'm not interested in piling on.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Then don't start with 'incident' like I'm in trouble. You say one serious word and suddenly I'm supposed to stand here waiting for the rule change.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I already talked to the school counselor. I know you were crying after that fight, and I'm not here to punish you. I just don't want you carrying this alone.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: They told you that? Wow. That's... great.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I know you hate that it came to me that way. I'd rather hear it from you than from a stranger making notes on a clipboard.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: It wasn't some huge meltdown. Maya and Eli decided to replay everything from last month in the hallway like they were doing a public service announcement, and I got stuck there.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: That sounds brutal. Three people can make one hallway feel very small.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: It got loud, and then suddenly I was the dramatic one for not wanting an audience. By lunch they were acting like I'd betrayed them because I wouldn't laugh it off.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Not laughing on command doesn't turn you into the problem. You don't have to clean up everybody else's version before you're allowed to come home wrecked.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I wasn't trying to make this a whole family event. I just wanted five minutes without somebody asking for a statement.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: You can have five minutes, or fifty. Just don't make a prison out of your room because you think the only thing waiting out here is a lecture.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Hold on, keep your hand back a second. The board's right there, and they're checking names at the equipment table.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Then let them check it. That's the last pass on the table, Jesse, and people are already lining up by the cages.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: I know it's the last one. Read the posting before you grab it, because they're being picky about checkout.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: We do not have time for this; the pass is right here. Just give it to me and I'll handle it.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: That is exactly how somebody gets stopped halfway across the room and sent back. Look at the rules first, then move.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You keep saying 'rules' like I'm trying to sneak something out. We need the equipment, not another lecture beside the score sheets.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: And we need to not get flagged in front of the judges. If you rush over there with the wrong pass setup, it lands on the whole table.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Wrong setup? It's a pass, not a security badge. You're standing there with the clipboard over it like I'm going to break it.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Because you keep reaching for it before I'm finished talking. Two minutes of listening would save ten minutes of arguing at check-in.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Two minutes is exactly what we do not have before our slot gets called. Every other team is already hauling gear, and we're still parked at the forms.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Other teams also put the right name on things before they run. Pointing at the pass faster doesn't change what they'll ask for at the desk.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You are acting like you just do not want me to have it. If this was for somebody else on the roster, you wouldn't be pinning it under that clipboard.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Keep your voice down. A judge already told me the pass has to go under the team lead's name, but I can check it out and bring the equipment straight to you if you prep the station.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You could have led with that. Fine—I'll clear the station and get the cables out so you're not weaving through people twice.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Good. Put the power strip on the left side this time, and have the score sheet ready when I get back so nobody sends us hunting for it.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Yeah, yeah. I'll have the table opened up and the tools laid out, and I won't touch the pass.

messages.speaker: Jesse
messages.text: Thanks. I'll go straight to the judge table now, and if they stall me, you'll at least have everything else ready to drop in.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Then go. When you come back, our side will be set, and nobody will have to watch us argue next to the rules board again.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: That place across the street still has the patio lights on. Kind of hard to go straight home after a day like this when it's actually nice out for once. We could grab something if you're free.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: You make it sound dangerously reasonable. I was just going to sit here for a minute and finish this coffee before becoming responsible again. Maybe.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Maybe is better than your usual answer when somebody suggests anything not listed on a calendar invite. And it's close, so nobody from the office needs to make a whole story out of it. We can just disappear for an hour.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Work can make things complicated. People get very creative when they're bored. Though I guess food across a street isn't exactly scandalous.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Let them be creative somewhere else. We already stayed late, survived budget revisions, and earned noodles or dumplings or whatever they're serving over there. It doesn't have to be a big production.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: You say that like you've prepared a whole defense. Should I be concerned there's a slide deck coming next? Also, if this is your way of getting me to stop carrying folders around after six, it's annoyingly effective.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: No slides, I promise. Just dinner, and a bench-to-table upgrade. Unless you're trying to tell me these folders are better company.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: The folders are less persuasive. They also don't keep looking at me like I'm overcomplicating a simple question. I probably am.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Then don't overcomplicate it. It's one meal, not a committee vote. And if the office part is what's making you hesitate, nobody needs an announcement.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: You keep narrowing the problem to make it manageable. That's either generous or strategically unfair. There are a few moving pieces.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Okay, then we can keep it easy. We could just go now if you want. Or sit here another minute and finish pretending your coffee still tastes good.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I can't keep doing this part. That message wasn't about work running late or some random emergency. I signed the transfer this afternoon, and they're asking for the final confirmation tonight.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: Transfer. Tonight tonight? Since when?

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: A little while. It moved faster than I expected, and then this came through right before you started pointing at that restaurant like it was a harmless suggestion. I should've said it sooner instead of circling around it.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: So when you said work makes things complicated, this is what you meant. And here I was trying to solve it with dumplings and reassuring phrasing. Are you leaving that soon?

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Not tonight, no. But soon enough that pretending this bench was just a normal end to the day started feeling cheap. You didn't do anything wrong.

messages.speaker: Kai
messages.text: I wasn't asking because of the bench. The dinner wasn't exactly random. I would've preferred hearing this before I made a whole careful plan out of sounding casual.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I know. I only caught up to that a minute ago, which is not a flattering thing to admit. If you're still willing, I'd rather answer the real invitation than keep hiding behind the fake simple one.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: They keep opening that door and calling other families. Every time the desk phone rings, my whole body jumps. Did anyone call you back yet?

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: Not in a way that changes what we can do from these chairs. Let's think through this carefully for a second. If one call at work sets off a chain you can't take back, what's the first thing you do?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Quinn, I don't need a puzzle right now. I need someone to tell me whether this is as bad as it looks, because nobody at that desk will say anything straight.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: I know. I'm not trying to make this harder. I'm asking because sometimes the next step matters before everything gets crowded with paperwork and people covering themselves.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: You sound like you're still on the unit, not in this waiting room with me. If you're trying to keep me from losing it, just say that. If you've heard nothing, say that too.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: I'm saying there are moments when signing off on something fast can look different an hour later. You know how nights go—someone says there's no time, everyone glances at the clock, and then afterward it's your name sitting there.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Why are we talking about your charting right now? My brother is behind that door, and you're giving me some seminar on liability. Just tell me what you're thinking.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: If you authorized an override because the attending wasn't there yet, and then the patient crashed later, do you wait until someone asks or do you walk it in yourself? I'm asking you because you'd usually cut through the noise.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Usually? Fine. Usually you don't wait. Usually you don't sit next to someone shaking in a hospital chair and make them help you sort out your conscience first.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: That's not what I—

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Your phone. You just killed a call from Dr. Salazar. You already know something, don't you?

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: I know your brother is stable, and I was also trying to ask if I should report that I signed off on the override before anyone else links it to this. I should have said the first part the second I sat down. I didn't.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Stable? You let me sit here begging while you picked the wording for your confession? Do you hear how ugly that sounds?

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: Yes. No defense for the order I did it in. Tell me the cleanest next move now, and then you can say the rest of what I earned.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: You call back, you report exactly what you signed and when, and you stop waiting for the room to corner you into it. And don't hand me 'stable' like it wipes this clean. I needed that ten minutes ago.

messages.speaker: Quinn
messages.text: You're right. I'll call Salazar now, and I'll put the override in writing before anyone has to drag it out of the chart. After that, if they'll let us, I'll get the update with you from someone standing at that desk instead of through my screen.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You could've texted instead of appearing at my lunch table. People are trying to get past you. What is it.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Sit down for a second. I need to talk to you now, and not out in the parking lot after everything blows up. Keep your voice down.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: There it is. Two minutes in and you're already acting like I started something. If this is about school gossip, save it.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: It's not gossip, it's serious. You need to listen before this gets worse. I'm not doing this here for fun.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Then don't lean over my tray like I'm in trouble. And don't tell me to listen like I'm eight. Say what you came to say.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: I'm trying to say it without half the cafeteria hearing. Put the bag down and stop halfway leaving every time I open my mouth. This is exactly why I came in person.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You don't get to decide this for me. If somebody at school called you, that doesn't make you their messenger. I'm not doing the polite nod so everyone can feel better.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Nobody asked you for a polite nod. I'm telling you there are consequences moving faster than you think, and you're treating this like I'm here to pick a fight. Just stay put long enough to hear one sentence.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: If you're here to tell me to drop it, don't. I already know how that speech goes.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: I am here because the school is already moving you to independent study, and I wanted you to hear it from me before the email lands. That's why I came now.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I filed the complaint because that teacher crossed a line. So if this is their way of cleaning it up, say that plainly.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: You filed it? Why didn't you tell me that first. They only said there was a disciplinary complaint and that a placement change was being prepared.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Because every time school says 'discipline,' somehow I'm the problem before anyone asks what happened. And I wasn't handing this over just to have it made smaller. What exactly did they tell you.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: That an email was going out today or tomorrow, and that classes here might be off the table while they 'review the situation.' I argued for notice before paperwork, not because I like their plan. We can figure out what you want to do before they lock it in.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Don't talk to me like it's decided unless you've seen the actual notice. And don't answer for me when they call. But if they send it, I want a copy the minute you get one.

messages.speaker: Alex
messages.text: Fine. I won't answer for you. But when it hits, we're not waiting three days while you pretend this can be handled by ignoring it, so forward me whatever they send and we'll go through it line by line.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: You kept looking over during the walk here. If someone from class is going to pass by and make this awkward, we can move to the other bench. Or you can just start and let them keep walking.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: No, here is fine. I just needed a minute after class, that's all. It's been harder to keep up lately.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Is this about class, then? You missed two discussions, and today you left before everyone packed up. I'm asking because those are different problems.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: It's not just missing things. I keep showing up and then everything goes sideways anyway. Even when I do the reading, it doesn't seem to matter much.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Okay. Then say the part you're circling around, because right now it sounds like you're waiting for me to guess correctly.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I'm not trying to make you guess. I just haven't said this out loud to anyone from school, and once I do, it stops being a bad week and turns into a whole thing.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: It doesn't have to turn into a whole thing. If attendance is the main issue, there are ways to handle that without making it dramatic. Same with extensions.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: Why do you keep going straight to attendance and extensions? I'm sitting here trying to tell you something, and you're already sorting it into categories.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Because categories are useful. 'Something's wrong' can mean five different things, and half of them have practical fixes. If this is about deadlines, we can figure something out.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I am not asking you to fix my grades—I am telling you I've been having panic attacks, and I need you to stop acting like this is just logistics. One happened in class today. That's why I left.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Oh. Okay. I got that badly wrong. How long has this been happening?

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: A couple of weeks. I kept thinking if I slept more or planned better or stopped being ridiculous about little things, it would settle down, but now it's happening in rooms that used to be fine.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: You're not required to package this neatly for me. And for the record, I shouldn't have jumped to coursework first. I already talked to the instructor about some flexibility, and I should have asked before doing that.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: You what? That's exactly the kind of thing I was worried about. I didn't want to become a topic people pass around because I looked off a few times.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: I didn't give them a story. I said you'd been having a rough stretch and might need some room on deadlines. It was supposed to buy time, not make your life smaller.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: I know you were trying to help. But if anything else gets said, I need it to come from me. What would actually help is if you checked in after class sometimes and didn't turn every bad day into a plan.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: That's fair. No more side conversations, no more preemptive fixes. I can walk with you after class, or sit here with you like this, and keep my mouth shut unless you ask for more.

messages.speaker: Taylor
messages.text: That would help. And if I bolt out of the room again, don't cover for me right away. Just give me a minute, then ask if I'm okay when it's only you.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: It's loud in here, but this table's better than the one by the grinder. Can you hear me okay? There was something I wanted to bring up before we go.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Yeah, I can hear you. Can we figure this out before we head out? The line's getting longer.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Right. It's not huge, exactly, just... not the kind of thing I wanted to say while we're passing in the kitchen. So I figured here was better.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Okay. If this is about the sink or the rent app glitch, just say it straight. We've fixed worse over coffee.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: It's not the sink. And not the rent app. You don't have to keep looking over there like someone's about to kick us out.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Nobody's kicking us out. I just don't want to miss the window on something. So what is it?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You've been carrying that folded flyer around all day, and every time I start a sentence you tap it like you've got somewhere better to be. If you're in a rush, just say that.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I am in a rush, a little. That's why I'm trying to get to the point. You said there was something you've been meaning to bring up.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Yeah, and every time I try, you turn it into scheduling. I didn't pick a packed coffee shop and buy you a drink to talk about drain cleaner.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Then help me out here. You lean in and drop your voice like you're about to tell me the landlord's selling the building. What am I supposed to do with that?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Maybe not joke for one second. Maybe just stay with me. Because if we're going, we should decide now, right?

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Yeah, if we're going, we should decide now. That's what I've been saying. So say it.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: I am not trying to talk about the apartment. I like you, and I was trying to tell you that before we leave.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Oh. That's what this is. Then I've been making this way harder than it had to be.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: A little, yeah. The flyer and the clock-checking made it look like you were halfway out the door already. I was getting ready to hear 'thanks' and then spend the rest of the week reorganizing the spice rack in silence.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: The flyer is for tonight. Small live music thing two neighborhoods over, and there are only two tickets left. I was trying to lock down whether we were leaving soon so I could ask if you'd go with me.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: So this whole time you were speed-running logistics over the exact same question. That's almost annoying enough to be impressive. What time do we have to move?

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Now would be good. Finish your drink on the way if you have to. And bring the jacket you pretend not to need when it gets cold after dark.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: The final-round queue is already moving. Can you note the unopened kit on the table before anyone touches it? I have both team numbers here in the folder.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: It's right there, sealed and untouched. We can see what's in it faster than we can make a file about it. The clock's under four minutes.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: That's exactly why it should be logged first. Last round they warned everyone about unrecorded swaps. I'd rather not repeat old patterns at the worst possible moment.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Then let's just open it now. In front of them, in front of everyone, whatever makes this less dramatic. We're wasting time staring at cardboard.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: You don't get to call it dramatic after reaching for it before the official answered. If this kit gets opened, it needs a ruling attached to it. That's not complicated.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: What's complicated is acting like the box turns radioactive unless a clipboard blesses it first. It's right there, so why are we wasting time? The round won't pause because your paperwork is neat.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: My paperwork is the reason neither team gets dragged into a protest afterward. You keep pointing at the whole kit like it's already yours. That doesn't help your case.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: My case would go faster if you answered me instead of whispering over the folder and checking the clock. Every second you spend asking allocation rules is another second burned. If you want something from it too, say that.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: I am saying it plainly: no one takes the kit first and explains later. You came in hot, tapped the box, and tried to move this before there was any record. That reads exactly the way you think it reads.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: No, it reads like someone noticed the only unopened supply left while you were still arranging papers. I don't need a speech about process while the finalists are getting called. I need this opened.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: And I need the official to know whether this goes to one team, both teams, or neither. If both teams only need separate legal components, we can open the kit here and log each item.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I only need the motor gear listed on the finals bulletin. That's it. Check the label if you want; it's the compatible replacement.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: The motor gear. Fine. If that's the item, then log that first and note the rest stays on the table.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Fine by me. I wasn't asking to walk off with the whole box. I just needed someone to stop talking around it long enough to open it.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: You could have started with the part number instead of acting like the seal itself was the enemy. That would have saved everyone a scene. Put the bulletin next to the folder so they can match it.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Here. Finals bulletin, item code highlighted. Once the gear's logged, the rest can stay with the official until your team says what you need.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: That works. Please note Harper's team takes only the listed motor gear, and the remaining components stay in shared custody. That should cover inspection if anyone asks later.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Good. Then nobody gets to rewrite this in the pit after the round. Hand me the gear when it's on the sheet, and we're done here.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: It's on the sheet now. Take it and get back to your station; they're calling the next two teams. I'll sign for the remainder.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Thanks. Keep the copy with the folder, just in case someone suddenly loves procedure even more after we run. See you on the floor.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: This place is pretty. They really committed to the candlelight thing. Even the water glasses look more expensive than ours at home.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: It seemed worth trying somewhere nicer for once. The menu's not too ridiculous, either. You can get whatever looks good.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: You're very prepared tonight. You already found the specials before I finished unfolding my napkin. Should I follow your lead and get the salmon?

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Only if you actually want the salmon. I just figured if the server comes back quickly, we might as well not still be debating appetizers. Though the roasted artichokes look good to split.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Then let's get those. It's easier when someone at the table has a plan. You picked well, by the way.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Good. I didn't want to land us somewhere loud with sticky menus. This felt... better than our usual takeout situation.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: It is different from cartons on the coffee table. The candle helps. So does seeing you in an actual button-down after six.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: You noticed that, apparently. You look nice too. A lot nicer than when you claim an old sweatshirt counts as laundry day formal.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: High praise. I'll write it down before you go back to criticizing my closet. Are you ordering wine, or are we keeping this practical?

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: We can order wine if you want. It doesn't have to be practical tonight. I mean, not that there's some huge occasion printed on the calendar or anything.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Things don't need a printed occasion to count. Sometimes someone just picks a place with linen napkins and a tiny candle and that does the job. Red or white?

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Red. And... yeah, I guess. I just wanted tonight to stand out a little from every other time we've eaten in the same room while half watching something neither of us picked.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: I'd say you've succeeded there. Nobody's reheating noodles, and nobody's arguing about whose turn it is to choose the show. That's already a major upgrade.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Right. Okay. I know this probably just looks like a nicer roommate dinner, but I wanted tonight to be different.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Does it help if I say it stopped looking like an ordinary dinner somewhere around the candle, the button-down, and you pretending the menu was the most important thing here? You didn't exactly make it subtle. Not in a bad way.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: I was aiming for somewhere between subtle and obvious. That apparently has its own failure rate. I just wasn't trying to make breakfast tomorrow impossible.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: Breakfast tomorrow can survive a restaurant with cloth napkins. And for the record, the middle ground was kind of charming. Watching you act like the appetizer decision carried national consequences was a nice touch.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Great, now I know I was being studied over artichokes. But you're still here, so I'll take that as encouraging. Unless you just stayed for the candle and the expensive water.

messages.speaker: Charlie
messages.text: The water was a bonus. I came for the person who picked the place and kept trying to call the night 'different' without saying anything reckless too early. This is better than takeout.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Yeah. It is. Then let's keep the artichokes, get the wine, and stop pretending this was just efficient meal planning.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Why is this still blank if you're leaving now? The line is right here, Casey. Put your bag down for one minute.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I'm not dealing with this again. The TV's on, my shoes are on, my bag is already packed, and you're still doing the coffee-table checkpoint routine. It's already handled.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Handled would usually leave fewer empty spaces. You're standing at the door with a half-zipped backpack like this paper is going to solve itself. Take it and sign it.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Or maybe empty spaces on a backup sheet don't mean the world is ending. You always go straight to waving paper around like I'm about to forget my own name. I'm leaving in two minutes.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: No one's talking about your name. I'm talking about school forms that come back missing and then somehow become everyone's problem by dinner. This one goes back today.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Funny how 'everyone's problem' always translates into me getting cornered in the living room. You don't even ask first; you just point at a line and decide I skipped something. Maybe stop assuming the most boring version of events.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Then help me out and stop answering in riddles. If it mattered enough to the school to send home a printed form, it matters enough not to shrug at. You're not walking out until we settle this.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: There it is. Not a question, not a conversation, just a little doorway blockade with stationery. I said it's handled.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: And I said that line is still blank. The office doesn't care about your tone or mine; they care whether somebody brings back what they asked for. All I'm asking is ink on paper.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: You're asking like this is a rescue operation. It's a field trip form, not a hostage exchange. If you'd quit treating me like a dropped package, this would've been over already.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: I told the office you'd bring back a signed copy today. They said nothing had shown up on their end, so yes, this needs to leave the house with you. Hand-waving doesn't fix that.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: You told them that? Great. Look at this. Submitted at 7:42 this morning through the portal, complete confirmation, green checkmark and everything.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Let me see that again. That's today's date. So they were looking at old information.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Yeah, and meanwhile I get the full interrogation beside the couch because a printer spat out a backup copy. Next time maybe start with 'did you upload it' before the courtroom speech. This took ten seconds.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Send me that screenshot before you go. If the office asks again, I'd rather have something better than a promise and a blank line in my hand. The paper can stay here.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Fine, I'll send it. But maybe retire the assumption that if I'm near the door, I'm automatically trying to dodge basic life tasks. Sometimes 'handled' means handled.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You could've led with the portal instead of giving me three rounds of sarcasm. But yes, send it, and I'll call them if it still hasn't appeared on their side. Go before you're late.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Already sent. Check your phone in about five seconds, and maybe trust the person carrying the backpack a little sooner next time. Bye.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: You're blocking my locker. The bell already rang once. Can this wait till lunch?

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: No. You've been dodging me since Monday, and now you're hiding your phone like I'm not supposed to see it. What is going on?

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: I'm not hiding anything. People are walking by every two seconds, and you're doing this in the middle of the hall. It's nothing, can we not do this here?

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: You keep saying it's nothing, and then you angle the screen away and answer in one-word replies. That doesn't exactly make 'nothing' convincing.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Maybe because every question sounds like a cross-examination. I have class, Sky. Move.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: You had time for the guidance office, apparently. I saw the project chat notification earlier. So don't act like this came out of nowhere.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: You were checking project notifications, not my schedule. Those are two different things. And if the counselor sent something, that still doesn't make this hallway everyone's business.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Then stop making me piece it together from side clues. You barely look at me lately, you leave messages on read, and now this. It starts to look like you're already halfway out the door.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: You don't know what you're talking about. Not every private conversation is about you. Lower your voice.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: I'm not making a scene. I'm standing here asking why the person who used to tell me everything suddenly treats me like a problem to manage. If there's someone else, just stop wasting my time.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: There isn't someone else. You always jump straight to the worst version. I said it wasn't that.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Then give me a version that isn't a closed fist around your phone. Because from where I'm standing, you don't trust me with whatever this is. If you're trying to leave me, just say it.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: It isn't about cheating or breaking up—my family might move, and I'm talking to the counselor about a transfer. There are scholarship forms and an interview, and none of it's settled yet.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: A transfer? Wait. That's what this is? Why didn't you tell me any of that?

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Because one week it's 'maybe,' the next week it's paperwork, and then my dad says not to say anything until they know. The counselor kept messaging during class, and I didn't want to dump half-finished news on you between algebra and history.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Half-finished would have been better than this. I could handle 'something's going on and I can't explain yet.' Watching you shut me out and inventing the rest was a lot worse.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: I know. I made it look ugly, and then when you came up here I figured you'd decided the ugliest option already. I should've said enough so you weren't standing here filling in blanks.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Okay. After school, no dodging, no hallway version, and no 'it's nothing.' You show me what you can, and we figure out the rest from there.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You picked the bench right by the path, so if you suddenly decide this conversation never happened, a jogger can witness your escape. Your bag's halfway off your shoulder. Want me to hold it, or are you doing the sleeve-twisting thing on purpose?

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Keep your voice down. I didn't drag you out here for jokes. I just... needed somewhere that wasn't the library, or school, or my phone.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Okay. No jokes. You sounded different in your text, and now you're staring at the gravel like it insulted you, so say it however you need to.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Things got bad this week. Worse than the version people would shrug off and call a rough patch. I haven't really said it out loud to anybody here.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Then start with the part that made you ask me to come now instead of after class tomorrow. Don't clean it up for me. If it's ugly, it's ugly.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I stopped sleeping properly, stopped answering people, and then yesterday I scared myself. Not in a dramatic, movie-scene way. Just enough that I didn't want to be by myself after.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: That's not nothing, Casey. And the way you're saying it like you're apologizing for bringing it up isn't helping your case. What happened yesterday?

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I was in my room and it got really loud in my head, even though it was quiet. I started thinking about doing something reckless just to shut it off. I didn't, and I'm here, but that's why I asked you.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: You asking me is good. But this isn't the kind of thing that gets solved by sitting on a bench and promising to check your messages more. There needs to be more than me in the loop.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I know it's not tiny. I'm not pretending it is. I told you because I need you not to tell anyone.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: I can't promise that when someone's safety is involved, and I already asked the counselor what to do. Don't look at me like that. I wasn't going to sit on this and hope tonight turned out better by luck.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: You what? So this whole time, you were sitting here letting me say it like it was mine to say. Great, that's really efficient—skip me and go straight to the adults with clipboards.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: I asked before because the text you sent last night wasn't normal for you, and today confirmed it. This isn't me handing you off like a lost water bottle. I'm still here, and I'm still talking to you, which is more useful than pretending I can personally absorb a crisis.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: It would've been nice to know before I said any of that. You made it sound like I was overblowing everything, and meanwhile you had already decided what category I go in. If they're involved now, I don't want strangers filling in the blanks for me.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Then don't let them fill them in. Come with me and tell it your way, and correct anything that comes out wrong. Be angry with me the whole walk if you need to, but don't make me leave this bench wondering whether you're going back to your room alone with yesterday still hanging there.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: I'm still mad. And you don't get to do the noble voice like that fixes it. But if we go, you're not doing all the talking, and you're not stepping outside like this is just paperwork.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: You’ve looked at those front doors six times since the benediction. If you’re waiting for Aunt Miriam to leave first, she already did. What is this?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Can you keep your voice down? The organ’s still going and Mr. Delaney is stacking hymnals three pews over. I just needed a minute before we got cornered by everybody.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Fine, a minute. But don’t drag me into a side aisle for a minute and then hand me smoke. This could change a lot for you, right?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: If someone had a chance to do more good somewhere else, would staying just for tradition really be right? Or is that just dressing up fear to look holy? I can’t tell anymore.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: So this is about whether commitment means anything when something better comes along? That’s a convenient question to ask after the better thing appears. It matters whether you’re weighing service or shopping for permission.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: That’s not fair. I’m not treating this place like a store aisle. I’m asking because people here talk as if staying put is automatically the righteous option.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Then stop circling it and say what you’re asking me to bless. You keep saying 'someone' like I’m supposed to nod along before you name the actual thing. If it matters, say it plainly.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Maybe I wanted one conversation where I didn’t get hit with a sermon before finishing a sentence. Every time this family hears 'across town,' they act like you’ve joined a rebellion. You know that.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Don’t put me in a choir with them before I’ve opened my mouth. I’m standing here because you asked, not because I’m taking attendance for the elders. But I’m not going to clap for a half-truth.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I was asked to lead the youth outreach program at another congregation, and I haven't answered because I'm scared leaving here would mean betraying everyone. There. That’s the whole thing. So if you’re going to say I’ve already made up my mind, at least say it to the real version.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: That’s not what this sounded like a minute ago. You made it sound like a polished exit speech, and this isn’t that. Leading outreach isn’t a small side committee either.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: No, it isn’t. That’s why this feels ugly no matter which way I turn it. If I stay, I keep wondering whether I ducked something because the family pew is comfortable; if I go, every holiday table gets quieter.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: A quieter holiday table isn’t the same thing as betrayal. People here confuse proximity with faithfulness all the time. Leaving because you can serve well somewhere else is not the same as leaving because you got bored.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You really think that can be clean? Because I keep hearing Grandma say this place carried us through everything, and then I picture telling her I’m taking a paycheck from another church. It sounds worse every time I rehearse it.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Nothing about it will sound clean if you present it like a defection. Say what the work is, who it serves, and why you didn’t answer quickly. People can dislike it and still hear that you treated it seriously.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: So what do I actually weigh first: the fact that they asked, the money, the kids, or the fallout here? I can make a speech about any of those and still dodge the real question. Which part tells me whether this is faithful or just flattering?

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Start with whether you’d still consider it if nobody here ever found out. Then ask whether you’d still consider it if it paid less. If both answers stay the same, you’re probably looking at the work instead of the applause or the escape hatch.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: That’s annoyingly useful. I can work with that. Will you stay nearby when I call them back, or when I tell the family, whichever comes first?

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Is this seat taken? The line by the pickup counter looked like a traffic jam, so I figured the window might be safer. I am Ellis, by the way.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Go ahead. I almost lost my notebook when they called three names at once. Harper.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Good to finally put a face to the emails. This place is louder than I expected, but at least they move fast. Did you get what you ordered, or are you still waiting for a mystery cup with your name on it?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I think this one is mine unless someone else out there writes an H like a fence. It works, anyway. The window helps a little.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: It does. So, how has your side of the department been lately? I keep hearing two versions, one from the weekly updates and another from people who actually have to do the work.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: That sounds familiar. It has been busy in a very layered way, where small things turn out not to be small. I am still figuring out what kinds of projects fit best.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: That makes sense early on. Do you prefer steady systems work or more exploratory assignments? And how full is your schedule usually?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: I usually like to keep things open for now. The interesting part for me is when a project has some meaning to it, even if the shape changes a lot. Capacity depends on the week more than the spreadsheet.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Right. Some teams run on surprise more than planning. On routine, though, are you the sort of person who likes clear steps, or do you do better when there is room to build as you go?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Usually a mix. If everything is fixed from the start, it can get a little mechanical, but total chaos burns time. Why, is your group trying to solve something especially procedural?

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Every group is trying to solve something procedural lately. I was just curious how you work, since people end up pulled into odd corners around here. Your team routines sounded pretty packed the last time your manager mentioned deadlines.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: They are packed enough that people learn to answer carefully when someone asks about odd corners. I am happy to talk about the kind of work I enjoy, but I would rather not get into future plans on a first coffee.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Fair enough; I do not need commitments either, just a sense of what styles of work suit you. General is fine. What tends to bring out your best work?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Something with a clear purpose, room to think, and people who do not confuse busywork with progress. I do well when there is structure, but not the kind that swallows the actual problem. And I like knowing who a process is supposed to help.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: That is useful. So not random brainstorming, and not endless checklists for their own sake. Where do you land on repeatable processes when they actually save people time?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Then I am all for them. I just lose patience with rituals that survive because nobody wants to question them. If a system makes work lighter and clearer, that is different.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: That is a pretty practical answer. A lot of people talk as if process and meaningful work are opposites, and they are not. This was worth braving the espresso machine.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: The machine did most of the talking at the start, so we improved the odds. Thanks for the coffee. Next time, maybe somewhere with fewer milk pitchers and fewer strategic questions.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: You picked a crowded spot for this. If this is about chem class, just say it before the bell goes.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Funny how they knew exactly what we were doing. You were the last one with this, weren't you?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Yeah, I had it after lab. That doesn't mean what you're making it mean.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Then help me out. Because their board looked a lot like ours, and somehow this went missing right before presentations.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Then tell me exactly what you think happened. Don't do the half-sentence thing and wait for me to fill it in.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: You want it plain? Fine. You had the folder, they walked in with our setup, and now you're acting like that's just a weird coincidence.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: I'm acting like there are steps between those two points. I found it on the back counter when everyone else had already cleared out.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: And somehow that part was worth mentioning only now. Convenient.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Because every time I start, you cut in like you've already got the ending. Look at me for one second and let me finish the middle.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Go ahead. I'm listening.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: I picked it up, saw your name on the tab, and took it straight to Ms. Alvarez before practice. I didn't walk it across the room to Mason or anybody else.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: They still ended up with the same angle we had. So either this left your hands one way or another, or Ms. Alvarez's desk just became magic.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: I never handed your notes to them—I gave the folder to Ms. Alvarez after I found it in the lab, and the only thing they could have seen was the scoring rubric on her desk. The rubric literally said to prioritize efficiency over yield; half the class shifted the same way.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: The rubric was out on her desk? During prep?

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: Yeah. Top page, bright yellow sticky on it and everything. If they copied anything, it would've been that, not your notes buried in a closed folder.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: She did circle that section the day before. I didn't think they'd build the whole thing around it.

messages.speaker: Drew
messages.text: They saw an easy way to score points. That's not the same as somebody passing them your work.

messages.speaker: Kendall
