messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Maybe. Hang on. Do you have a pen that actually writes?

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Yeah, but don't do the 'maybe' thing and then vanish at lunch. They still need people, and it'd look good for the service hours. Plus Ms. Alvarez always remembers who helped.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I know what it is. Can I borrow the pen? Just for a second.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: You know what's funny? You're standing here with your hand on the sheet like it's going to run away, but you're acting like I'm pitching a pyramid scheme. If you don't want to do it, just say that.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I'm not acting like anything. I'm asking for the pen. The line's moving in two minutes.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Okay, dramatic. Here. I'm just saying you keep checking the clock and giving me one-word answers like the idea personally offended you.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Thanks. Could you not lean on the board? I need the paper flat.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Seriously? I'm not blocking anything. Look, the Saturday shift is probably the easiest one anyway, and if you're worried it'll eat your whole weekend, it won't.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Hayden. One second. Please.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Fine, but you're making this weirdly difficult. I can't tell if you're dodging me or planning to stare at the sign until second period.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I'm writing. That's what I've been trying to do.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Oh. Wait— that's your name by the last slot. You were already taking it.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: There was one opening left. I said I'd fill it this morning if it was still there. The pen from the office died halfway through the first letter.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Wow, okay. I thought you were doing that thing where you make me talk until I give up. Sorry. Here, I'll stop breathing on the clipboard.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: It's fine. There. Done. I just needed that exact line before somebody else wrote over it.

messages.speaker: Hayden
messages.text: Got it. Next time I'll lead with 'do you need ink' instead of a sales pitch. Come on, let's move before we're both late.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Hey. Are you busy, or are you just making that pile look nicer than mine ever does? The TV's been flashing the same commercial for ten minutes.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: If you step on that sock, you're folding the next load. What's up? So what happened after school?

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Nothing dramatic. I got home later, that's all, and I figured you'd notice eventually.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You figured right. Start at the beginning and save me the trimmed version.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: It wasn't some huge thing. Friday got weird, and I didn't really want to walk in here and get jumped on the second I opened the door.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You're standing here now, and nobody's jumping on you. Friday got weird how?

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: School was just... loud. Everyone kept acting like everything was normal, and I needed a minute before coming home.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: A minute where? With who? Don't make me pull each word out one at a time.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: By myself, mostly. I walked around for a while, then sat somewhere, then came back. It wasn't like I disappeared for a week.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You're working hard to keep this blurry. 'Somewhere' and 'for a while' aren't answers.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Fine. I just needed some air after school.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: The counselor already called me. I know you left before last period with your bag, so please stop editing the story.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Oh. So this whole time you already had that. You could've just said that instead of letting me stand here sounding stupid.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I gave you room to say it yourself. Instead I got half a dozen soft edges and not one straight line.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I didn't skip because I felt like blowing off class. I left because if I stayed in that room one more minute, it was going to get ugly, and I didn't want my name attached to whatever happened next.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Then say that. Walking out with a bag and saying nothing buys you a bigger mess, not less of one.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: There was this presentation, and everyone was doing that thing where they smile at you before they start in. I packed my stuff before last period because I already knew I wasn't making it through the hour without either saying something bad or giving them a show.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: So you bailed before it blew up. I can follow that part. What I can't let slide is you coming in here and trying to sand it down until it sounded like a long walk.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I came in here with three different versions and none of them sounded safe out loud. The school calling you first made this worse, but at least now I don't have to keep pretending it was nothing.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Good. Next time, call me before you leave campus, and we deal with the school after, not the other way around. Hand me that towel, then sit down and give me the rest without cutting pieces off it.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Okay, I’ve got the checklist open on the left and the draft on the right. The lamp is blasting my face, so if I look squinty, that’s why. For this next section, do we move to outreach or the review pass?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Hang on a second. Before we jump there, I want to go back to that earlier checklist item. Something about the order needs a closer look.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: The order? I thought we already cleaned that up yesterday. If you want, just give me the next item and we can tweak the wording after.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: It’s not exactly wording. I was looking at the sequence again just now, and it doesn’t line up the way it should. I’d rather not keep building on it until we sort that out.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: So what’s the next step then? You keep hovering over that middle box like it’s cursed. If it’s just a label, we can survive one ugly label for ten minutes.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: That’s what I’m trying to prevent. If we use it as written, the handoff later is going to look strange. Let me straighten out where that change came from.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: I’m not trying to rush you, I just need something solid enough to keep moving. From my side, it looks like the list is mostly intact and we’re stuck on phrasing. Are we actually blocked, or is this cleanup?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: More than cleanup. I know it probably sounds like I’m dragging us sideways, but this is one of those cases where one shifted line turns into three bad decisions after it. So give me one minute on the earlier part.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Okay, one minute. I’m literally pointing at item three on my screen and waiting for it to become less mysterious. What changed?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Before we do the next item, I need to correct something: I reordered the checklist after misreading the lead's note, so the document is wrong and that part is on me.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Oh. That makes a lot more sense than what I was picturing. All right, then let’s fix the order first—what did the lead actually mean?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: The review pass was supposed to stay before outreach, not after it. I read the note like they were asking for a full reshuffle, and I changed the shared doc before double-checking. So item three and four need to switch back.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Got it. I was reading your pause like you were trying to polish the list before answering me, and that was clearly not the situation. I can swap those now if you want to call out anything else tied to them.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Yeah, thanks. Once those two are back in place, the sub-bullets under outreach need to sit under review instead, at least the first two. After that, the next step is straightforward again.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Done on the main swap, and I’m dragging the sub-bullets now. This actually explains why the timeline looked lopsided when I tried to map it earlier. Can you check whether the dependency note still belongs under item five?

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Yes, item five stays where it is. The dependency note is still correct; it was the order above it that threw everything off. The checklist should read cleanly now.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: It does. All right, with review back before outreach, the next step is the review pass, then we send the summary after that. That tracks much better.

messages.speaker: Dakota
messages.text: Exactly. Thanks for stopping with me on it instead of charging ahead on the bad version. Now we can use the list without it steering us somewhere weird.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Hey. Sorry, parking was a mess, and this place is louder than I remembered. You got here a while ago?

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: A few minutes. Long enough to order. You picked a crowded spot.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Yeah, well, neutral ground seemed smart. Do you still get the same thing here, or did I already miss my chance to pretend I know your routine?

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: It's a drink, Ari. Not a personality test. What did you want to talk about?

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: We can get to that. I just— it's been a weird few weeks, and every time we only talk when something's on fire, it goes badly. How's work?

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Still work. Computers break, people panic, I fix it. Efficient cycle.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: Right. You always did like things that can actually be fixed. Mom said you've been helping her with the insurance forms too.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: She called. I answered. That's not exactly a headline.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I know. She just mentioned it because she appreciated it. People notice more than you think, even if they don't always say it well.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: That's a new line from this side of the table. Did she also mention why you asked me here instead of just texting whatever this is?

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I didn't want it to come out wrong. And texting would've made it colder than it already might sound. I was trying to do this face-to-face.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: You keep talking around it like there's a hostage negotiator in your ear. If it's bad, then it's bad. If it's just inconvenient for you, that's different.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: It's not about convenience. I just wanted five minutes where neither of us jumped to the worst version of the other. That's apparently harder to arrange than I hoped.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: If you came here to tell me something after everyone else already knows, just say it instead of treating me like I'm the problem.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: They know? I— I'm moving in two weeks. It's for a job, and I should've told you before anybody else heard it from me.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Of course. That's why the careful tone, the little pauses, the scouting the room first. You had the whole script ready except the part where I get included before Mom and whoever else.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: You're right about that part. I let too many people hear it before you did, and that lands exactly as badly as it sounds. I kept putting this off because the last few times I brought big news, we ended up throwing old injuries at each other.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Then say that, not all the warm-up exercises. I can handle hearing something straight. What gets old is being managed like there's always a cleanup crew waiting behind me.

messages.speaker: Ari
messages.text: I'm sorry. You should've gotten it straight, and from me, before the family grapevine turned it into another performance. For what it's worth, I wasn't trying to sideline you; I was trying not to make the distance worse and managed to do exactly that.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Well, you did. But at least this is the first sentence tonight that sounds like you brought me here for a real conversation. Next time, start there.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: You picked the only bench in the park that isn't wet. That's either luck or a setup. Go on, you keep looking around like someone's about to overhear state secrets.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I wanted somewhere we could actually stop for a minute. And the ducks are louder than half our neighbors, so that helps. This won't take long.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Whenever someone says that, it takes exactly long enough to become my problem. If this is about the apartment, just say that first.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: It does affect the apartment, yes. I was trying not to drop it badly. There's a timeline attached.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: A timeline. Great. So we're doing the part where you've mapped something out and I get invited in after the blueprint's done.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: That's not what I'm doing. I wasn't looking for you to approve anything, and I wasn't trying to corner you. I just needed to tell you before it got any later.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Good, because I'm not signing up for a last-minute reshuffle because you want a different arrangement. If something's changing, say what changes. Spare me the careful preface.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I got offered a job in Portland, and I already accepted it, so I'll be moving out in about six weeks. I found out fast, and then it all moved faster than that. I should have said it sooner.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Portland. That's not exactly across town. Six weeks is also not exactly generous notice.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I know. That's why I wanted to talk before rent, before viewings, before any of that became more complicated. I'll cover whatever needs covering on the way out.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: You're very efficient when the decision's already made. I was bracing for a pitch about next year, not a completed exit. That's a different kind of courtesy problem.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: If I tried to turn it into a committee meeting, you'd hate that too. I wasn't hiding it to make your life harder. I was trying to figure out how to say it without making it sound like I was running from the place.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: The place isn't the issue. And for the record, I wasn't planning to renew the lease anyway. I've been looking at living alone next term.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You were. Okay. That would have been useful information about twenty minutes ago.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: You arrived with the face you use before dropping a spreadsheet on someone. It looked like I was about to get handed a plan with my name already typed into it. I wasn't in a rush to volunteer my own.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Fair. You looked ready to object before I opened my mouth, so I kept trying to frame it better. That obviously worked brilliantly.

messages.speaker: Lennox
messages.text: Brilliantly, no. Conveniently, maybe. We apparently both had separate escape routes and still managed to make this awkward.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Awkward I can work with. I'll send you the exact dates tonight, and we can sort the lease, furniture, and whatever else needs untangling. I'd rather leave the apartment in better shape than this conversation started.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Your coffee's gone cold. You haven't touched it once. Start wherever you want.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: They just pulled the rug out from under me, that's where. One minute everything's normal, next minute it's like the floor disappears and everyone acts like that's business as usual. And then you're supposed to sit there and nod.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Who did? Your manager? You keep tapping the table like you're trying not to throw something.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Does it matter which one of them said it first? The whole place had that look, like they'd already moved on before I even got out of the room. You'd probably say I should've handled it differently.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: I didn't say that. I'm trying to figure out what happened. Did something happen at work that you're not telling me?

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: See, that's exactly the tone. Like there's some neat little thing I did and if we find it, everybody can relax because then it's all my fault. It was unfair, Ellis.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: I'm not looking for a neat little thing. I'm looking at you sitting here wound this tight, and I know you don't call me in the middle of a weekday to stare at a latte. What actually happened?

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: I walked in and by lunch everything was upside down. They had their phrases ready, all polished, all empty, like they were doing me some favor. You'd probably say I should've seen it coming.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Maybe I would've said you should've documented something, or not mouthed off, or whatever people say after the fact. But I still don't know what I'm responding to. I can't help if you keep circling it.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: There it is. Help. A list, a budget, a lecture about backups and emergency funds and all the ways I should've been more like you. That's why I almost didn't come.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: I was going to say we can make a list of what to do, yeah, because that's something concrete and you're talking so fast I can barely keep up. But I stopped because you looked ready to bolt. I can't tell if you want comfort or a plan, and I'm afraid I'm getting this wrong.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Both, I guess. I got laid off, and I need you to not go straight into fixing me before you say you're sorry.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Okay. First, I'm sorry. Then we can figure out what you want help with.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Three days ago. I've been getting up in the morning and leaving anyway so nobody asks questions, which is obviously ridiculous now that I'm saying it out loud. Rent's due next week, and I still haven't told anyone else.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Three days is not very long to carry that by yourself. No wonder you look wrung out. Do you want me to just stay with the rent part first, or the family part?

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Rent first. Family can wait one more minute before it turns into a whole panel discussion. I really don't need Mom doing that careful silence thing and then texting links.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: Then rent first. I can cover part of it, and we can look at the rest only if you want another pair of eyes. Nobody else has to hear anything tonight.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Part would help. Even hearing you say it like that helps more than I expected. I kept rehearsing this version where you asked what I did wrong.

messages.speaker: Ellis
messages.text: I wondered if there was more to the story, but not in that way. You were talking like someone bracing for impact. Next time, you don't have to spend three days pretending before you call me.

messages.speaker: Sage
messages.text: Next time, maybe don't open with detective voice and the mug grip. But yeah. Maybe next time I call before the coffee goes cold.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: You can keep the chair there. It's a crowded table, not exactly private property. Just don't act like nothing's weird.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Okay, that is an aggressively formal welcome for a cafeteria with spilled fries on the floor. If this is about me dropping my tray here without asking, I can do the whole ceremony and back out.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: It's not the tray. Though the casual entrance does fit the theme. Amazing how smooth people get when they already know the script.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Now I'm definitely missing a page. You looked at me like I stole your parking spot, and we're indoors. What exactly am I supposed to have the script for?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Maybe for the part where somebody gets turned into a punchline and then gets asked why they're being dramatic. That scene usually lands great with an audience.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Whoa, okay, so this is not about chair etiquette. Did somebody say I said something, or are we talking about something you actually saw? Because those are two very different disasters.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Interesting choice, putting 'actually saw' in there. Makes it sound like there are options on the menu. I caught enough earlier.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Earlier when? At the counter? In line? You're going to have to give me more than a trailer cut, Sam. I can't fix a mystery accusation between tater tots and a fire drill.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Your phone was on the table by the napkin dispensers. I wasn't trying to snoop; it was right there. My name was on the screen next to something generous and flattering, apparently.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: My phone? Wait, the screenshot? Is that what this has been about? Hold on.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: There it is. 'Hold on' like context is a magic trick you pull out after the reveal. Convenient timing.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: No, seriously, look at it. Wait, you mean this screenshot? Scroll up one line. Don't stop at the part you saw.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Oh. That was copied from someone else. And right under it— 'That's unfair to Sam.'

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Yeah. I sent it because people were piling on, and typing the exact line was the fastest way to shut it down. You only caught the middle of it, didn't you?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Apparently I picked the worst possible frame. I've been sitting here sharpening knives over half a sentence. That's spectacular.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Honestly, with just that slice, I get why you came in hot. You could've just said 'hey, why is my name on your screen' before turning lunch into a courtroom drama, though.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Yeah, well, opening with that in the middle of a room full of people didn't sound brilliant either. And the whole calm-tray-down, point-at-the-chair routine wasn't helping your case.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: I thought you were annoyed I barged into your table space. Then you kept glaring at me like I'd kicked your backpack, so I started guessing dumber and dumber. This version makes way more sense.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: For the record, the backup glare was ready for the backpack theory too. But, fine, that one's on me. Next time I'll aim for the full screenshot before building a prosecution.

messages.speaker: Jordan
messages.text: Great, and next time I'll lock my phone before it starts side quests. Truce? Also, your fries are about to get stolen by the sophomore orbiting this table.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Your aunt's name just popped up again. You can turn the radio down more if you want; I couldn't tell if you were trying to hear it buzz.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: It's just family. Seat belt's twisted by your shoulder.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I got it. If this is about what I said, I can explain.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: This is exactly why I don't like people stepping into my family stuff. We just left the driveway.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I wasn't trying to make a scene. She cornered me by the dessert table and kept going on about next month.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Let's not do this right now. I need to watch the road, and I don't need a committee meeting in the car.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Okay, but the silence isn't exactly helping. You looked at the phone like it already answered the question.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Because with them, it usually does. There's always a plan, and somehow I'm the last one supposed to hear it plainly.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I wasn't lining up with anybody. I just didn't want her penciling you into something before she'd even asked.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Then maybe don't have side conversations with my relatives about what I should or shouldn't be doing. That never lands cleanly.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: So that's what this is. You think I made you look incapable.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I think every time they smell an opening, they shove. And then I get to clean it up while everybody acts helpful.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I only told her not to dump hosting on you because you've already been stretched thin. That's all I said.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: So this is about what you said? She already texted me that you were too sensitive and that I should host instead.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: She said that? And you sat through dinner with that in your pocket while she kept smiling at me across the table.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I wasn't giving her the satisfaction of turning the whole afternoon into a spectacle. Then your aunt lights up my phone before we've hit the first stoplight.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I shouldn't have pulled her aside. I thought cutting it off there would keep them from piling one more thing onto you.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Next time, bring it to me first. If they want an answer about dinner, they can get one from both of us and not through whispers over pie.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Fine. Then both of us can tell her next month isn't hers to assign, and she can keep the commentary about me to herself.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Good. I'm not hosting because someone decided for me, and you're not getting volunteered as the family weather vane either. Let her text all she wants until we get home.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Your iced tea is mostly melted. We probably sat here longer than I thought. That kid's been looping past us with the same scooter for ten minutes.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: You always notice patterns like that. Mine's still cold enough, somehow. It gets breezy near the path once the sun starts dropping.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Yeah. It's quieter when the dogs head home and the runners take over. I kind of wanted the extra few minutes before we go back.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Before we go back to the apartment? Okay. You sound like you're working up to something, so just say it plainly.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: I was trying to find a version that didn't come out badly. And every version sounded worse if I kept rehearsing it. So this may be clumsy.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Then I'll save us both some circling. I don't date people I live with, and I don't want us to blur lines just because we get along.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Wow. Okay. I wasn't trying to pressure you—I was going to tell you I like you, but mostly I needed you to know so I could stop acting weird.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I jumped ahead. That's on me. The way you started sounded like there was going to be a proposal attached to it, and I answered that before you finished.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: No proposal. No five-point plan, no persuasive closing argument. Just an explanation for why I've been suddenly fascinated by washing dishes when you're in the kitchen.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: That does explain a lot, actually. I thought you were avoiding me over the electric bill or because I kept stealing your good pan. I'm sorry I made it sound like you'd done something out of line.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: You did steal the good pan, but that wasn't the crisis. And for the record, I knew this might land nowhere. Keeping it unspoken was getting stranger than saying it once and dealing with the fallout.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Saying it once is fair. I should be clear too: that line wasn't invented on this bench. I keep home and romance in separate boxes now, and that's not something I'm opening up for exceptions.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: That's a real rule, then, not a custom rejection with my name on it. Weirdly, that helps. Stings, but it helps.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: It's real. And if I'd let you finish first, it probably would have sounded less like a courtroom ruling. You didn't deserve to get cut off at the knees for trying to be honest.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: I've definitely survived worse than an overefficient boundary speech. Honestly, the worst part was thinking I'd made you look at our place like a problem. I didn't want the couch, the coffee mugs, all the ordinary stuff to suddenly feel loaded.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I don't want that either. I like our ordinary stuff exactly because it stays ordinary. If anything needs adjusting, we can name it instead of doing that careful doorway dance you've been doing all week.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: That doorway dance was subtle and sophisticated. Also completely obvious, apparently. I can retire it.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Please retire it. And keep using the kitchen when I'm there, even if I have the pan you like. I'd rather deal with a little awkwardness than with silence stretched across the whole apartment.

messages.speaker: Reese
messages.text: Deal. We go home, make dinner, and pretend this bench isn't now historically significant. Maybe in a month it can go back to being the place where you judged that guy's running form for twenty minutes.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I was right about his shoulders, by the way. And yes, we go home, make dinner, and let this become one honest conversation instead of a strange season. You can have the good pan tonight.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Hi, Casey. You found the place easily, then. This table's quieter than the front.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Hi. Yeah, I got here a little early, so I grabbed this one before the rush. The lighting's nice back here.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Good choice. They packed the tables near the window too close together. Have you been here before?

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Once, a while ago. I remembered the bread was good, which feels like the main thing. Sorry, one second.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Of course. Busy week? You look like you've been pulled through a few directions today.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: It's been a day. Nothing very interesting to report, just one thing after another. How was yours?

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Structured, mostly. Meetings, revisions, the usual parade of people changing adjectives in documents. Do restaurant first meetings usually go on your list of interesting things, or not especially?

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: That depends on the company, I guess. I don't really rank them like that. Sorry, I keep checking this.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: I noticed. We can order quickly if you're on a clock. Or keep this short if that's easier.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: No, it's fine. I said I'd be here, so I'm here. You don't need to rearrange anything.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: Right. So how has your week been, besides busy?

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: A little uneven, I guess. Work stuff, family stuff, the usual pileup. Nothing I can explain neatly over a menu.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: If you'd rather be somewhere else, I'd rather you just say that. Polite endurance isn't necessary.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: That's not what this is. My aunt was taken to urgent care about an hour ago, and I got the call after I'd already left home. Canceling at the last minute felt awful, so I came anyway and kept waiting for an update instead of making this strange from the first minute.

messages.speaker: Marlowe
messages.text: I shouldn't have put it that way. That explains the phone. If you need to leave, call, or sit here until you hear something, we can do exactly that.

messages.speaker: Casey
messages.text: Thank you. I didn't want this to look careless. If we start over a little, I'd like that.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I can see the deadline banner on the shared screen, so let's keep this tight. I've got the budget tracker open and the approvals log beside it. What specifically are you missing on your end?

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: The current budget file, not the summary tab from last week. The numbers in the deck stop short of the latest approvals, and I can't finalize vendor decisions from screenshots. My access still shows denied.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Access to that folder follows the standard approval path. Once approvals are confirmed, permissions are updated through ops rather than by whoever happens to be presenting the material. That's the route in place for everyone.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: So who exactly has the authority to grant it, then? Because the deadline is on the screen, and we're talking about work that depends on that file already existing somewhere with current numbers. I'm trying to understand why this is still sitting in limbo.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Ops executes the permission change after finance marks the version approved. Let's stay with the standard approval path instead of jumping ahead of the log. If you need a specific field in the meantime, I can read it out or export a limited view.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Reading it out on a call doesn't really solve the problem. I need the actual approved file attached to my workstream, not fragments passed across in pieces. Otherwise every change turns into another meeting.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: No one is suggesting you work from fragments long term. I'm saying there is a sequence, and it matters because this file feeds three teams and an audit trail. If I bypass that casually, it becomes a different issue.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Casually isn't the word I'd use. This started before today's call, and every answer so far sounds like it's coming from a handbook instead of from the actual situation in front of us. The actual situation is that I'm blocked and the project isn't.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: The actual situation is also that approved financial files aren't distributed informally just because a date is close. I'm looking at the notes now, and the last recorded step says pending access alignment after approval confirmation. That's why I'm being precise.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Fine, then let's be precise. I already have an older copy from Maya, so I know the file exists; I need the current approved version and to know whether my access was intentionally restricted.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: You have a copy from Maya? That's not how that file should have moved. And no, your access was not flagged under some separate instruction with your name on it; the folder was narrowed when finance shifted the approval chain last week.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: That would have been useful to hear about eight minutes ago. If the folder was narrowed across the board, then say that plainly. The silence around it made this look narrower than that.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I'm saying it plainly now: the restriction sat at the folder level, not at your seat. Maya shouldn't have circulated an older version, which is part of why I was careful about this on a recorded call. The current approved file can be added through a documented request today.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Okay. Then I need the documented request sent while we're here, and I need the approved version tied to it so I'm not building from two-week-old numbers. I'm not going back to the team with another maybe.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That's reasonable. I'll submit the access ticket before we end and copy finance so the approval stamp is attached in the thread. Once ops processes it, you'll have the live file rather than another export.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Send me the ticket number too. If anyone asks why the projections shifted, I'd rather point to the approved version than explain why I was piecing things together from old material. That should keep the rest of this cleaner.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: You'll have the number in a few minutes, and I'll note that the prior version circulating was outdated. For what it's worth, the request itself wasn't the problem. The way it landed made it harder to answer quickly than it needed to be.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Right. Well, now there's an answer I can use. Once the access comes through, I'll update the deck and keep the rest inside the thread.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: You picked the bench by the pond. Still the one with peeling green paint. So what exactly did you want to say?

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: It seemed neutral enough. Less likely to turn into a scene with joggers doing laps two feet away. Thanks for coming.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I was already nearby. You said it mattered, so here I am. Go on.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I wanted to clear something up. Not in the five-texts-and-disappear way things usually get handled now. This seemed harder to misunderstand.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That's an interesting choice of phrasing. Were you seeing someone then or not? Because that would clear up a lot very quickly.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: You always did prefer the shortest path between two points. I get why you're asking it like that. The problem is the shortest path tends to skip the parts that explain why everything looked the way it did.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: What it looked like was pretty straightforward from where I was sitting. Messages got thinner, plans got vaguer, and then people started saying things. You didn't exactly rush in to correct any of it.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: No, I didn't. By then every conversation felt like it arrived already decided, and I handled that badly. But there is a difference between handling something badly and the version that kept circulating.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: If you only called me here to explain yourself, just say that. I'd rather hear the efficient version than watch you build a footnote.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: Fine. Read this. I did not cheat, but I should have told you sooner that the rumor was false. I know I also shut down and made everything look worse.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: This is from Maya? "I made it sound bigger than it was" isn't subtle. Then I should stop treating that rumor like the whole truth, but I still need you to admit how distant you were.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I can admit that. Near the end, talking to me probably felt like knocking on a locked door and hearing me move around inside. That part belongs to me.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: It did. Every answer sounded trimmed down to the minimum required for survival. So when that story reached me, it fit too neatly with everything else.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: That's the piece I underestimated. I kept assuming the facts would eventually sort themselves out, which was convenient for no one. Meanwhile silence kept doing unpaid labor for the worst interpretation.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: You had a talent for making absence sound temporary. "Just busy," "just tired," "not great at texting"—all of it left plenty of room for other people to finish the story. They did.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: I know. And I let that happen because saying anything directly would have required more honesty than I was offering at the time. Not about another person—about how far gone we already were.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: That would have been brutal, but at least it would have been yours. Instead I got fragments, and apparently one of them came with commentary from Maya. That's not exactly a satisfying archive.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: No, it isn't. I brought the screenshot because I didn't want you leaving with that part still lodged where everything else had already done enough damage. The rest doesn't get erased by that.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: No, it doesn't. But it's different, and different matters. I can put down one accusation without pretending the ending was kind.

messages.speaker: Riley
messages.text: That's fair. I wasn't kind, and I wasn't clear, and those are plain enough words to leave here with. If this was the last missing piece, I'm glad it isn't missing anymore.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Can you turn the radio down a second? Or I can. There's something I should probably mention before you get on the highway.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Go ahead. We're stopped anyway. So what is this about?

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Don't make this a big thing, okay? It's not bad, exactly. I just got an email chain finalized about a program.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: A program where? You can talk it through if you're weighing options. No need for the dramatic setup.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Seattle. Research track, computational cognition lab, better equipment than here. It kind of came together faster than I expected.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Have you compared funding and housing yet? Seattle gets expensive fast. And 'kind of' usually means there are details doing a lot of work.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: The stipend's decent, and they help with first-year housing. That's not really the difficult part. Timing is more awkward.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Then the timing is the part to sort out. If you're thinking about applying or interviewing, say that. Half the stress disappears once it's specific.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: It's already specific. I already said yes to the program in Seattle last week. I just didn't say anything yet.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Last week. Okay. Then I guess funding and housing aren't theoretical.

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: No. I was going to tell you earlier, but there kept being people around, and then it started sounding stranger the longer I left it. That's not a great system, apparently.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: Apparently not. When do you leave? And are you keeping your spot in the lab here until the semester ends?

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: End of December, if the paperwork clears on time. I'll finish the current project remotely after that unless Dr. Singh objects. I wasn't trying to make this look sneaky.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: You signed paperwork before mentioning it in the car on the way home, so it does have a look. But December gives you time to hand things off properly. Have you told Singh yet?

messages.speaker: Frankie
messages.text: Not yet. You first, then him. That order probably doesn't improve my case much, but there it is.

messages.speaker: Harper
messages.text: No, it doesn't. Tell him tomorrow, make a transition list, and send me the housing spreadsheet if you want another pair of eyes on it. We'll keep it organized.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Hey, Emerson? Good, I picked the right table. This place is louder than it looks from the sidewalk, so thanks for grabbing a spot.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: You found it. Go ahead. If the espresso machine starts shouting again, we can always move farther back.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: I kind of like the chaos up here. It makes first conversations easier when nobody can hear every word. Did you already get something, or were you waiting to see if the line got less ridiculous?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: I don't wait on lines to improve. They usually don't. I got coffee, and that's generally enough to tell me whether a place knows what it's doing.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Practical. That tracks. So, are you still the type who reorganizes a whole project board before touching the actual design work, or have you relaxed a little?

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Depends who's asking and why. But no, I don't confuse improvising with efficiency. You sound pretty certain for someone opening with coffee.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: I just like people who know how they do things. It's rare. And I heard you used to make impossible deadlines look routine, which is either talent or very good bluffing.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Interesting wording. People usually pick one version when they don't know me. Which did you have in mind?

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Probably both, if we're being honest. The old design team sounded like a circus from the outside, and you kept it moving, so that says something. Not everyone can do that without making enemies.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: You already asked Maya about me, so I'd rather you just be direct than pretend this is all off-the-cuff. If you're going to arrive with a file, at least put it on the table.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Okay. I did ask her. It was brief, and it sounds worse now that it's out loud, but I didn't want to walk in completely cold and step on a land mine five minutes in.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: You could have led with that. Quiet research tends to land differently when the subject hears tailored questions dressed up as coincidence. It saves time if we're not doing that.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Fair. I tried to make it smooth, and that was the part that made it messy. Maya made it sound casual, like everybody asks everybody about everyone, and I took that advice farther than I should have.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: Everybody does plenty of things I don't make room for. Direct works better with me, even when it's awkward. Especially then.

messages.speaker: Phoenix
messages.text: Then here's direct: I wanted this to go well, and I overproduced the opening scene. No more scavenged details. Ask me something back, or tell me where you want to start, and I'll keep it clean.

messages.speaker: Emerson
messages.text: All right. Start with something you didn't workshop on the walk over. Then we'll see whether this coffee shop gets credit for the reset or whether you do.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Morning. You picked the only room with nowhere to hide once people start circling the glass. Do you want these reports here or out of your line of sight?

messages.speaker: Logan
messages.text: Here is fine. Sit, if you have a minute. I was reviewing the staffing ramp and the cost spread, and there are gaps.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: There are always gaps at this stage. The question is whether they're the kind that slow a team down or the kind that disappear once delivery starts moving. This plan still gets us momentum the other schedules don't.

messages.speaker: Logan
messages.text: Momentum doesn't answer overtime exposure. Or contractor dependency in week four. What am I missing in these assumptions?

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You're starting from the downside column. If we keep the current pace, we lose the client window and end up paying for drift instead of compression. The team can absorb more than your spreadsheet is giving them credit for.

messages.speaker: Logan
messages.text: Can they absorb it, or can they absorb being asked to say they can? Those are different things. I'm looking at a half-finished model because the inputs don't line up.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You brought me in, closed the door, and opened with week-by-week risk. That usually means the verdict was drafted before the meeting invite went out. If you want a list of weak points, I can save you some time.

messages.speaker: Logan
messages.text: If I wanted a list for display, I wouldn't have asked before the room fills up. I asked you here because I have to advise on the timeline in ten minutes, and I need to know whether these numbers are solid.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Those printouts are already wrong—Finance updated the cost model this morning, and I came in trying to stop you from using them. I should have led with that instead of letting you keep tapping the old assumptions.

messages.speaker: Logan
messages.text: That would have been useful about five minutes ago. Fine—show me what changed. Start with labor and contingency.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Labor goes up less than this version suggests because Finance reclassified two specialist roles into the existing headcount pool. Contingency is narrower, but only if procurement holds the vendor rate through the first milestone. The ugly part moved from staffing to timing on approvals.

messages.speaker: Logan
messages.text: So the compressed schedule isn't automatically reckless; it's conditional on procurement and approvals not slipping. Why weren't these revisions circulated?

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Finance sent the revision to directors first and promised the broader packet by noon. I grabbed what I could before walking over. If this goes upstairs on the old packet, the conversation turns into theater.

messages.speaker: Logan
messages.text: All right. Then I need a clean sentence I can use that doesn't overclaim and doesn't sound like we're improvising in public. Give me the threshold where the two-week cut still holds.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You can say the reduction is supportable if procurement confirms vendor pricing today and approvals stay inside the current review window. If either slips, the savings flatten and the schedule benefit erodes by the second sprint. That keeps it narrow without underselling it.

messages.speaker: Logan
messages.text: That's better. Send me the revised model as soon as Finance releases it, and forward whatever note you got this morning. I'd rather not walk in with yesterday's argument dressed as today's data.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You'll have it before anyone sits down. And for what it's worth, if you flag the approval dependency first, nobody can accuse you of polishing it. It lands cleaner coming from you.

messages.speaker: Logan
messages.text: Noted. We'll keep it to the dependencies and the updated assumptions, nothing ornamental. Thank you, Shiloh.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You called from ten feet away like this couldn't wait two minutes. I'm right here, and the box is on the table if that's what this is about. So go on.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Okay, because I saw the delivery notice and then I saw that behind you. You can't just open a package when we don't know whose it is. If it's for another unit, that's a whole thing.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You started with pointing, so I'm guessing you've already got a verdict. I opened the door, brought it in, and checked it. That's the whole dramatic story.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Checked it after cutting it open, apparently. That's exactly what I'm saying should've waited. There are literally labels for a reason.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Right, labels exist. That's usually why people look at boxes before holding a trial over video chat. Anything else?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Don't do that clipped thing where you act like this is normal. If it's not ours, then opening it is not some tiny whoops. I just don't want the apartment getting dragged into something dumb.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: The apartment is going to survive one cardboard box on a coffee table. You're making this sound like I was rifling through a neighbor's mail for fun. Can you slow down for one second?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: I'm slowing down, you're just not answering the part that matters. You should have waited before tearing into it. Leaving it unopened would've solved everything.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Solved what, exactly? Because from where I'm sitting, you're arguing with a story you made up the second you saw tape peeled back. You haven't even asked what's in it.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: What's in it doesn't change whether you were supposed to open it first. And the way you're sitting there with it still out makes it look like you're trying to act casual until this blows over. That's not helping.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: I'm sitting in a chair, Jamie. The box is out because you pinged me and said get on camera now, not because I'm staging evidence. There's a difference.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Then just say whose box it is. Because all I'm hearing is pushback on the easy part and nothing on the obvious part. If the address was off, this gets messy fast.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You keep saying 'if' like nobody here has actually looked. I did. More than once, since apparently that matters now.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: And somehow that was less important to mention than sarcasm? Great. From over here it looked like you opened something random and decided it wasn't a big deal.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Jamie, did you even look at the shipping label? It's your name on the box, and the charger from your email receipt is inside.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Wait. The replacement charger? The one for the old laptop brick? I thought that wasn't supposed to come until tomorrow.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Apparently it came early. Same store name as the confirmation email you left open on the kitchen counter this morning, same last four digits on the order number. I was trying to tell you before you built a whole crime scene around it.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Okay, wow. Then that is completely on me. I saw the open box, filled in the rest, and came in way too hot.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Yeah, a little. Next time maybe start with 'what's in the box' before the lecture. But fine, now at least we're talking about the actual box.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Fair. Sorry for coming at you like that. Keep the charger there for a second, I'll grab it when we're done, and maybe I retire from package detective for the night.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: If you're looking for the warranty papers, they're not on the coffee table anymore. I put the important stuff in the folder by the couch, so don't shuffle it around. I just need two minutes.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: I'm not looking for a warranty. Why won't you just tell me what's in that folder? You've been guarding it all afternoon.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Because every time paperwork shows up in this house, you turn it into a trial. There's a note right there—read that first. Then we can stop circling.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Am I supposed to sign this without context? It says we both agree to hold off talking to Mom, and somehow that's presented like it's routine. What exactly am I agreeing to cover for?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You're agreeing not to blow this up tonight. That's all. We can deal with the rest after dinner, after she's done pacing around about the plumber and everything else.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: You keep saying 'the rest' like it's a minor footnote. Just say what the problem is. If it's simple, you wouldn't need a signature before a sentence.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: It's not a courtroom exhibit, Sky. It's a practical step so one thing doesn't become six things in an hour. Sign it, and then nobody has to perform outrage in the living room.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Don't do that. You don't get to slide paper across the table and act like questions are theatrics. We're not done.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Move, then. I need to put these away before she comes in and starts sorting through stacks like she's inventorying a fire. You're making this bigger than it needs to be.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: That's interesting, coming from the person half-hiding a folder under utility bills. If this is so manageable, open it. Let me see what requires my name but not my knowledge.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: You always go straight to motive like that's the only useful category. Fine. You want the order reversed so badly, here.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: A bank notice? Overdue? River, what did you do?

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: The late payment happened because I moved the money to cover the repair bill, and I needed your signature so we could buy time before talking to Mom. The car was already in pieces, the contractor wanted cash that day, and there wasn't some magical third option sitting in the drawer.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: So this wasn't just missing paperwork. You made the call, hid the notice, and handed me a note like my part was to bless it afterward. That's a hell of a way to ask for help.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: The repair couldn't wait, and neither could the payment on that invoice. I should've said it before the note, yes. I'm saying it now, and the number on the notice is still sitting there whether you glare at me or not.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Then here's what happens now: no more papers pushed at me first, no more edited versions, and no delaying the conversation just because it's inconvenient. Show me the repair bill, show me the account, and then we decide what to tell Mom together.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Can we talk about earlier before this gets worse? The dishwasher's been open for ten minutes and neither of us has put in the last plate.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: What did you want to say? If this is about my family again, just say it.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: It's about us trying not to keep doing this in the kitchen after every family dinner. I need to understand what happened.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: A lot happened. You were there for most of it. Unless there's a part I missed.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I'm not doing a cross-examination. You went quiet, then your sister left early, then your mom said that thing at the table, and after that it felt like I was standing in the wrong room.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Maybe because everyone kept acting like there was a script and I hadn't been given a copy. You looked pretty comfortable with it.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Comfortable isn't the word I'd use. I tried to slow it down, and you started stacking plates like you could scrub the whole evening out of existence.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: And now we're back to me handling things wrong. That's efficient, at least. You can just say you think I made a mess.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I'm saying I was shut out, not that you're some disaster. There's a difference. I can't help with something when I only find out by reading everyone's face at dinner.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You want the version with numbers, then? Fine. I already promised my sister some money, and I was scared you'd think I chose them over us.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I called your mom earlier because I wanted to fix what happened, and she said none of this was meant the way we thought. I don't love being left out, but I want us to set limits together.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You called her? That's not where I thought this was headed. But that sounds a lot different from what was sitting in my head all evening.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Your mom said she was trying not to embarrass your sister, and it landed badly with everyone. That doesn't erase you keeping this from me. It does mean I'm not here to make you choose between people.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: It's three months, not forever. Rent, groceries, and getting her through that gap before the new job starts. I should've brought it to you before I gave her a number.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Then let's talk about the number now, and what happens if three months turns into five. I can work with helping; I can't work with surprise debts and weird dinners.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Okay. We can put an actual ceiling on it, and if anything changes, it doesn't wait until someone's passing mashed potatoes to come out. I'd rather this stay between the two of us than get filtered through the whole family again.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Can you open this line before everyone walks in? The allocation for the pilot, right here. If it isn't live when the deck gets to slide twelve, this whole table of numbers turns into decoration.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: No, not before the meeting. Leave the sheets there. The deck is already up, and we're not rewriting the room in the next two minutes.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I'm not asking for a rewrite, I'm asking for access. You're standing at the laptop like it's a vault, and this is the one line they are absolutely going to ask about. We can fix it now instead of doing theater in front of the glass.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: What we can do now is stop jabbing at paper like that changes the timing. I said not before the meeting. Use the approved figures on the printout.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: The approved figures are the problem. They make it look like the project stalled when it didn't. If this is about wanting a cleaner justification first, you've had the justification since Tuesday.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: This isn't getting decided by who repeats themselves harder. People are already lining up outside, and I'm not flipping anything because the clock got loud. Bring the discussion with what cleared.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: You're making it sound like I'm trying to sneak something past you. I'm trying to keep the meeting from turning into twenty minutes of side-eye over a number that could be changed in ten seconds. If there's some extra hoop, say that instead of parking on no.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: And you're making it sound like this is me guarding a toy. It isn't opening before the meeting. That's the answer.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Then what exactly am I supposed to say when they ask why the allocation is sitting there untouched? Because 'Kendall said no' is not going to land well. Especially when you're one click away from it.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Don't put this on a single click. You want a reason, fine. Give me a second.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: I'm giving you a second. I'm also looking at three people pretending not to watch us through the wall. So yes, a reason would help.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: It is not a judgment call from me—the line is frozen by finance until compliance clears it this afternoon. Look at the screen. See the hold code and the timestamp?

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Oh. That wasn't on the print packet. Okay, that lands a little different.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Yeah. I should've started with that instead of batting your hand off the budget sheet. For the meeting, say the allocation is under same-day review and the operating work keeps moving under current approvals.

messages.speaker: Sutton
messages.text: Fine. I can work with 'same-day review' a lot better than a blank number and a stare-down. After this clears, send me whatever version finance won't have a heart attack over.

messages.speaker: Kendall
messages.text: Done. I'll pull the note and the cleared line as soon as the hold drops. For now, keep slide twelve tight and don't promise the room money that isn't unlocked yet.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: You brought a folder to a restaurant. The plates are still empty and we're already doing this. I should have guessed from the corner table.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I asked for someplace quiet because the office wasn't helping. I needed you to see the bigger picture before this hardens into something worse. That's why the folder's here.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: There it is. The bigger picture. Every time that phrase shows up, my part gets reduced to a footnote.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Your part isn't a footnote. The proposal was moving people very quickly, and there were things in it that couldn't just slide by because everyone liked the presentation.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: This is about you overruling me again. You said ethics in the meeting, closed the door on it, and left me standing there while leadership looked at me like I'd brought in a toy.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: I wasn't trying to make you look small. I was trying to stop a decision before it landed on the team. You keep pulling this back to rank when the contract is the issue.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Did you ever plan to treat me like a partner here? Or was dinner just a cleaner place to deliver the closing argument with linen napkins instead of conference-room glass?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: If I wanted a closing argument, I would've left after ordering. I'm still here because I don't want this sitting between us every time a vendor comes up. Can we stay with what was actually in front of us?

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: What was in front of us was a recommendation I put my name on, and then you cut it off without even letting me answer the room. You sat there calm, like the verdict had been written before I opened my mouth.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Calm wasn't what it looked like from my side. I saw a line in that paperwork that crossed a boundary, and once I saw it, I couldn't pretend timing would fix it. I kept waiting for a way to explain that without turning the meeting into a spectacle.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: You keep saying boundary like I'm supposed to fill in the rest. You already decided I couldn't be trusted.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: No. Look here—this clause lets them use employee data far beyond implementation, and the consent language is buried under the training appendix. I blocked it because this clause would let them exploit employee data, and I didn't tell you sooner because I learned you had personally championed them upstairs and I didn't want to expose you in front of the team.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: I never saw that appendix cross-reference. They walked me through the dashboard and pricing for an hour and skipped this entirely. Why keep this to yourself after the meeting?

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: Because saying it in that room would've turned your recommendation into a public demolition. And afterward, every version of the conversation sounded like either I was covering for you or talking down to you, so I did neither and made it worse.

messages.speaker: Micah
messages.text: Worse, yes. If a clause like this is sitting there, I need it in front of me before the floor drops out under my name. Don't make that call for me again.

messages.speaker: Morgan
messages.text: You're right. Next time, you get the document the moment I flag it, and we deal with the fallout together before anyone else gets the room. I can live with a difficult conversation a lot more easily than this version.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: So waters go on the back station first, then the extra rolls under the host stand? I'm just making sure I heard you over the dishes. It's loud back here.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Right. Waters filled before doors, rolls under the stand, and check table twelve's wobble before anyone gets sat there. Keep this side clear so runners can cut through.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Got it. And if a table gets sat while I'm already carrying entrees, do you want me to greet first or let someone else touch it for a second?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Greet first if you can do it in passing. If not, tell the host you're behind by a minute and don't disappear on the food. Tonight won't wait for perfect timing.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Okay. For the handhelds, do orders go straight in at the table here, or do people usually step to the server station first?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: At the table if it's clean and quick. If the guests are still deciding, move on and circle back. Don't get pinned while the board starts stacking.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Makes sense. If I ask where something is mid-rush, who should I grab without getting in someone's way?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Nearest person with a free hand, or me if it's about your section. Salt's by expo, extra check presenters are in the second drawer, and coffee cups live nowhere sensible. You'll find the rest fast.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Right. Sorry, that's probably basic stuff. I can just figure it out as I go.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: No, ask now—I need you to tell me when something is unclear, because tonight I'm deciding what I can trust you with. If you stay quiet and guess wrong, that helps nobody. So ask.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Okay. Then where do you want me if a four-top gets dropped on me while the kitchen is already backed up? I don't want to play catch-up three minutes in.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Then you start with the greet, drinks, and whatever buys you a clean next pass. If the kitchen's dragging, use that instead of hovering at the screen. And if you're about to get buried, say it early and I'll shift a table before it turns ugly.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: That's useful. One more thing: if I get stuck on the POS and it looks like I'm taking forever, do you want me to wave you over or send the host for you?

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Wave me over. I'd rather untangle it in ten seconds than find out after tickets are wrong. Same with anything guests ask that sounds small but can snowball.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: All right. Then I should probably ask the dumb version now—what mistakes actually get under your skin out there? I can work around a lot better if I know that part.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Hidden ones. If a server is slammed, fine, I can work with that; if a server goes silent, I can't. Late is fixable, sloppy can be fixed too, but surprises spread.

messages.speaker: River
messages.text: Fair enough. Then if I look lost, I'll say lost instead of pretending I'm taking the scenic route to the coffee cups. And if table twelve starts rocking, I'll catch it before somebody wears a soda.

messages.speaker: Jamie
messages.text: Good. Take the two booths by the window and the four deuces along the rail to start, and keep me updated before you need rescuing. If you handle those cleanly, I'll open the rest to you.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You got quiet all of a sudden. Is this about the exam, or are you about to ruin my fries?

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: Keep your voice down for a second. I heard something about Monday's exam, and I don't want this bouncing around the whole restaurant before we even know what it is.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Okay. You're looking at the receipt like it's evidence, so just say it.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: Someone from our section said they saw Mateo with the test bank open on his laptop before class. Maybe it was old material, maybe it wasn't, and that's exactly why I'm bringing it up carefully.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: If that was the real bank, that's not small. People studied honestly for that exam, and someone needs to take this to the instructor.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: Slow down. I don't think we should go report someone based on this when it came to me through one person at another table in the library.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: So what, we just pass the ketchup and pretend we never heard it? If no one says anything, people who cheat just keep winning.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: That's not what I said. I'm saying rumors turn into labels fast, and once that happens, you don't get to pull it back because you were trying to do the right thing.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: But this isn't random gossip about who hooked up with who. It's a class grade, and everybody else in that room gets measured against it.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: And everybody else in that room also gets to exist without being dragged in front of a professor because someone 'heard something.' There has to be a line before that.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: You're making it sound like the only options are public shaming or silence. There are ways to flag something without turning it into a spectacle.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: Then name one that doesn't start with Mateo getting called in over a story neither of us witnessed. Because the minute his name is attached to this, it stops being abstract.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: If you keep this quiet because you don't want drama, you're protecting cheating, not being careful.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: I care about not accusing someone without proof. That's not the same thing, and you know it.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: Fine. Then not a direct report from us. The person who actually saw the screen could talk to the instructor, or even send what they saw without dressing it up like a verdict.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: That's different from marching in there with a name and a conclusion. If anything happens, it should come from the person who was there, with exactly what they saw and nothing added.

messages.speaker: Shiloh
messages.text: I can live with that more than doing nothing. And if they won't say it themselves, at least tell them not to keep dropping it into side conversations like it's harmless.

messages.speaker: Avery
messages.text: That's fair. I'll talk to them and make it clear this doesn't get repeated table to table like tonight's special.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: You picked a great spot for an audit. Joggers, dogs, a clipboard-looking folder. Very community theater.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: It's a folder, not a prop. And this wording cannot stay. The line about the council knowingly poisoning the neighborhood is the problem.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Of course that's the line you circled. It's always the sharpest sentence that suddenly becomes inconvenient once it might make someone uncomfortable.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: People will dismiss us if this sounds exaggerated. Then the rest of the flyer goes with it, including the testing data and the meeting date.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: There it is. Make it neat, make it safe, make it digestible for the people who prefer their harm politely phrased. Every time you make it safer, it stops saying what is wrong.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: I'm asking about one sentence, not the whole campaign. We can say the council ignored warnings, delayed action, and left residents exposed, because those points are documented.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Documented enough for your standards, maybe. The rest of us don't need a notarized confession to recognize what happened. If that's too much, maybe this whole version should be scrapped then.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Scrapping it helps no one. We have volunteers ready to hand these out Saturday, and I'm not spending another week rebuilding something just because you refuse any revision.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Any revision? No. The kind where everything turns into passive verbs and tasteful outrage, yes. Funny how your pen always lands on the sentence with a pulse.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: I am not asking you to make it milder. I am asking you not to print a claim we cannot defend, because if one line is false, people will dismiss everything else we are trying to protect.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: So this isn't about making the flyer sound respectable. It's about not handing them an easy lie to point at. That's different from sanding the whole thing down.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: Yes. Keep the indictment if you want; just anchor it to what we can show. "Ignored contamination reports" hits hard and survives scrutiny.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: "Ignored contamination reports" is solid, but it still lands like a memo. What about "ignored contamination reports while families kept drinking from those taps"? That's in the timeline too.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: That works if we cite the dates underneath. Then the sentence carries weight without giving them a technical escape hatch. Put the health clinic number beside it and people know what to do next.

messages.speaker: Wren
messages.text: Fine. And the headline stays bigger than the city logo you wanted, because this is still an accusation, not a brochure. Hand me the pen instead of hovering with it.

messages.speaker: Skylar
messages.text: The logo can shrink. The claim gets tightened, the sources go at the bottom, and these can still go out Saturday. That's all I came here to settle.

messages.speaker: Parker
